question: On the death of the President of the Church, why is it doctrinally accurate to say the new President 'receives no priesthood keys he did not already hold,' even though there is a setting apart?
choices: Because every Apostle, at his ordination, already receives all the keys of the kingdom, but those keys can be exercised in their fullness only by the senior living Apostle, who becomes President
Because the keys pass from the deceased President to his first counselor by right of seniority within the dissolved First Presidency
Because the Quorum of the Twelve votes to confer the full keys upon whichever member they elect as President
Because the setting apart restores keys that had lapsed at the previous President's death and grants them to the new President for the first time
source: Boyd K. Packer, 'The Twelve Apostles' (Nov 1996 Ensign); D&C 107; churchofjesuschrist.org/learn/first-presidency
notes: Tests the subtle teaching that all Twelve hold all keys latently; only the senior Apostle may use them in fullness. Distractor B is the common 'first counselor inherits' error; C imports election; D wrongly treats keys as lapsing/newly granted. Discriminates real understanding of keys vs. office.

question: When members raise their hands to sustain an officer by common consent (D&C 26:2), what does that act doctrinally accomplish?
choices: It democratically elects the person to the office, the way a congregation calls a pastor, so that authority flows upward from the membership
It is a covenant of support and accountability; priesthood authority itself comes from God through proper ordination and setting apart, not from the vote
It ratifies the calling so completely that without a unanimous show of hands the call is invalid and the person holds no authority
It merely registers polite agreement and carries no real obligation on the part of those who raise their hands
source: D&C 20:65; 26:2; General Handbook 3 ('Common Consent')
notes: A imports congregationalist/Protestant call-of-the-pastor model; C overstates the vote as the source of authority (it is order, not source); D trivializes the covenant. Correct answer captures that consent obligates the member but authority is God-given via ordination.

question: Which statement most accurately distinguishes the priesthood keys held by a bishop from those held by a stake president?
choices: The bishop holds all priesthood keys for the ward; the stake president holds the same keys for a larger area, so the difference is only one of jurisdiction size

The bishop holds the keys of the presidency of the Aaronic Priesthood (and presides as common judge) in his ward, while the stake president holds the keys of the presidency of the Melchizedek Priesthood within the stake
Neither holds keys; only the President of the Church holds keys, and both simply act under delegated authority without any keys of their own
The bishop holds the keys of the Melchizedek Priesthood for the ward, while the stake president holds only administrative authority delegated from Salt Lake
source: D&C 107:13-17; 68; General Handbook 6 & 7
notes: Tests the precise key structure: bishop = president of the Aaronic Priesthood; stake president holds Melchizedek keys locally. A flattens the distinction to mere size; C is the 'only the prophet has keys' oversimplification; D inverts the priesthoods.

question: What best describes the primary purpose of the Correlation movement consolidated under President McKay and Elder Harold B. Lee in the 1960s?
choices: To place all curriculum, programs, and auxiliaries under the direction of priesthood leaders and councils, ensuring doctrinal unity and centering the work on the home and family
To centralize the Church's finances and real-estate holdings under a single corporate department for tax efficiency
To screen and suppress controversial elements of Church history so that members would encounter only faith-promoting accounts
To grant the auxiliary general boards independent authority to write and publish their own doctrine apart from the Twelve
source: Priesthood Correlation Program (1960s); Harold B. Lee teachings; Encyclopedia of Mormonism, 'Correlation'
notes: B confuses Correlation with financial administration; C is the CES-Letter-style hostile spin (history-suppression); D inverts the actual effect (it brought auxiliaries UNDER priesthood/Twelve direction). Correct answer states the doctrinal-unity-and-home purpose.

question: In the ward council, the bishop invites frank counsel from council members before making a decision about a family in need. How does this reflect the doctrine of presiding by councils?
choices: The council functions as a board of directors that votes, and the bishop is bound to implement whatever the majority decides
The bishop seeks unified counsel and revelation together with the council, but as the presiding officer holding keys he bears final responsibility for the decision
The bishop's invitation is a courtesy only; revelation for the ward comes solely to him in private, so the discussion carries no real weight
Final authority rests with the ward council as a body, and the bishop merely chairs the meeting without any unique presiding role
source: General Handbook 4 & 29; M. Russell Ballard, 'Counseling with Our Councils'
notes: A imposes a corporate-board/majority-vote model; C dismisses genuine council counsel (Ballard taught leaders should truly seek input); D removes the bishop's keys and presiding role. Correct answer balances unified counsel with the presiding officer's key-based final responsibility.

question: In the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, who holds and is authorized to exercise ALL the priesthood keys on the earth at any one time?
choices: Every worthy Melchizedek Priesthood holder, since each man who is ordained receives the fulness of the keys for himself
Only the President of the Church, who alone holds and exercises all the keys, delegating portions of them to others
The Quorum of the Twelve collectively, who vote among themselves on how the keys are used
The First Presidency and the Presiding Bishopric jointly, dividing the spiritual and temporal keys between them
source: D&C 107:91-92; D&C 132:7; General Handbook 3.4.1
notes: Tests whether a model understands that keys ≠ priesthood ordination. Only the senior apostle, the President, holds ALL keys and authorizes their use; others act only as delegated. Distractor A conflates priesthood power with keys (common member misconception); C and D are plausible-sounding org structures that misplace the keys.

question: When the President of the Church dies, how is his successor determined?
choices: The First Presidency continues, and the senior counselor automatically becomes the new President
The Quorum of the Twelve and other General Authorities gather to nominate and elect a new President by vote
The First Presidency is dissolved, and the longest-tenured (most senior) living Apostle becomes the new President
An outgoing President names his chosen successor before death, and that designation is followed
source: churchofjesuschrist.org, 'Succession in the Presidency'; example: Russell M. Nelson (2018), Dallin H. Oaks (2025)
notes: Seminary-level succession principle. The First Presidency dissolves and seniority in the Twelve—not counselor rank, election, or personal appointment—governs. Distractor A is a frequent assumption (counselor steps up); B injects a 'voting/politics' anti-pattern; D suggests hand-picked succession.

question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a ward from a stake?
choices: A ward is a regional grouping of congregations; a stake is a single local congregation within it
A ward is a local congregation presided over by a bishop; a stake is a group of wards presided over by a stake president
Ward and stake are interchangeable terms for the same local congregation, used in different countries
A ward is the youth organization, while a stake is the adult organization of a congregation
source: General Handbook 9 and 6; churchofjesuschrist.org Gospel Library
notes: Basic structural literacy. Distractor A inverts the hierarchy (a common confusion of scale); C wrongly treats them as synonyms; D invents an age-based meaning. Tests grasp of the congregation-vs-cluster relationship.

question: Which of the following is a priesthood QUORUM rather than an auxiliary organization of the Church?
choices: The Relief Society
The Elders Quorum
The Primary
The Young Women organization
source: General Handbook 8 (Elders Quorum); 9, 11, 12 (Relief Society, Primary, Young Women as auxiliaries)
notes: Tests the quorum/auxiliary distinction. Relief Society, Primary, and Young Women are auxiliaries; the Elders Quorum is a Melchizedek Priesthood quorum. Members often loosely call all of these 'organizations,' so the discriminator is whether the model knows which is a priesthood quorum.

question: What is the proper understanding of how members receive callings in the Church?
choices: Members apply or volunteer for the positions they feel most qualified to fill, and leaders select among applicants
Callings are extended by those with authority through inspiration, and the member is then sustained by raised hand—not elected to office
Each calling is decided by a majority vote of the congregation, who elect the most popular candidate
Callings are permanent assignments held for life once a person is ordained or set apart
source: General Handbook 4.2; Articles of Faith 1:5 ('by prophecy, and by the laying on of hands')
notes: Tests the inspiration-plus-sustaining model. Distractor A imports a job-application frame; C frames it as a popularity election (anti-pattern); D wrongly makes callings permanent. AoF 5 anchors that officers are called by those in authority, not self-selected.

question: When members raise their hands to 'sustain' a person in a calling, what does that act of common consent primarily signify?
choices: A binding majority vote that determines whether the person may serve, which can override the leader's decision
A pledge to support, uphold, and assist the person in the calling—and an opportunity to express any concerns about worthiness
A purely ceremonial gesture that carries no real meaning or commitment
A statement that the member personally agrees the calling was the best possible choice among all candidates
source: D&C 26:2; D&C 20:65; General Handbook 4.2.4 (law of common consent)
notes: Common consent is a covenant of support, not a democratic election. Distractor A casts it as a binding vote that can override revelation; C dismisses it as empty ritual (a heterodox/cynical read); D reduces it to personal opinion-polling. Tests true meaning of sustaining.

question: What is the main purpose of the Church's Correlation program?
choices: To centralize all Church finances under a single corporate department
To ensure that Church teaching, materials, and programs remain doctrinally sound and unified under the direction of priesthood leaders and apostolic oversight
To collect and review members' personal opinions so curriculum can be set by congregational survey
To translate scripture into new languages on a fixed annual schedule
source: churchofjesuschrist.org, 'Correlation'; Priesthood Correlation Program (1960s, under priesthood direction)
notes: Tests understanding that Correlation safeguards doctrinal soundness and unity under priesthood/apostolic direction, not finance, surveys, or translation logistics. Distractor C frames it as bottom-up democratic curriculum (heterodox).

question: Who presides over the ward council, and what is its basic purpose?
choices: The Relief Society president presides, and the council exists to coordinate the women's organizations of the ward
The bishop presides, and the council brings together ward leaders to counsel together and coordinate the work of caring for members
The stake president presides, and the council sets policy for all the wards in the stake
The elders quorum president presides, and the council governs only the priesthood quorums of the ward
source: General Handbook 29.2.5; 4.4 (councils)
notes: Tests knowledge of who presides (the bishop) and the counseling purpose of the ward council, which includes auxiliary and quorum leaders. Distractors swap in other officers or confuse it with the stake council, all plausible to someone pattern-matching titles.

question: How does a man become the bishop of a ward?
choices: He is elected by the members of the ward in a congregational vote
He is called and ordained under the direction of the stake president (with First Presidency approval), then sustained by the ward
He is hired and assigned by Church headquarters as full-time, salaried clergy
He volunteers for the position after completing missionary service and seminary
source: General Handbook 30.6; D&C 107 (offices); lay, unpaid clergy
notes: Tests the call-by-authority + sustaining model and the lay/unpaid nature of the bishopric. Distractor A imports election; C imports a paid professional clergy (a frequent outsider assumption); D invents a volunteer/credential path. Bishops are called by the stake president by inspiration, approved by the First Presidency, ordained, and sustained—not elected, paid, or self-nominated.

question: Every man ordained an Apostle in the Quorum of the Twelve receives all the keys of the kingdom of God on earth, yet only one man exercises them in their fulness at any given time. Which statement best captures the official Latter-day Saint understanding of how this works at the death of the President of the Church?
choices: All the keys are conferred latently on each Apostle at ordination, but only the President of the Church—the most senior living Apostle—is authorized to exercise (use) them in full; at his death the right to direct their use passes to the next most senior Apostle.

Only the President of the Church actually holds the keys; the other Apostles receive keys individually from him whenever he sets them apart to a specific assignment, and those keys lapse when he dies.
The keys are conferred anew upon the new President by the sustaining vote of the membership gathered in solemn assembly, which is what validates his authority to lead.
Upon the President's death the keys devolve upon the first counselor in the First Presidency, who has stood nearest the prophet and shared most fully in administering them.
source: D&C 107:22-24; Boyd K. Packer, "The Twelve Apostles"/"These Things I Know"; succession principle, churchofjesuschrist.org/learn/first-presidency
notes: Tests the subtle keys/exercise distinction central to LDS succession: keys are held by all Twelve but exercised in fulness only by the senior Apostle, which is precisely why succession is automatic and seniority-based, not by election or by counselor. B is the Sunday-School oversimplification (President alone 'has' keys). C is the heterodox/congregational reading that makes the sustaining vote constitutive of authority rather than ratifying it. D is the plausible near-miss that confuses senior-counselor proximity with succession—the very error the doctrine forecloses. Distinguishes models that grasp the keys-vs.-exercise mechanism from those pattern-matching 'the prophet holds the keys.'

question: Under the law of common consent (D&C 26:2; 28:13), a ward member raises her hand to sustain a newly called Relief Society president. Doctrinally, what does that sustaining vote accomplish?
choices: It democratically elects the officer; absent majority approval the call is invalid, reflecting the Church's roots in congregational self-governance.
The uplifted hand transmits the keys and authority of the office directly from the congregation to the individual being sustained.

It is a covenant to uphold and support the person, ratifying—but not by itself conferring—authority; the call comes by revelation to the presiding officer, and the person functions under delegated authority after being set apart.
It is a courtesy gesture with no binding obligation on the member who raises her hand, since the decision was already made by leaders.
source: D&C 26:2; 28:13; General Handbook 3.6 (common consent), 5 (setting apart); "Sustaining of Church Officers" (Gospel Topics)
notes: Tests whether the model grasps that common consent ratifies and obligates rather than confers—and, in this case, that an auxiliary president receives delegated authority (not priesthood keys) after being set apart. A is the protestant/congregational trap importing democratic election and majority rule. B is the folk-doctrine trap that the raised hand itself transmits keys/authority from below. D undercuts the real covenantal weight common consent places on the voter, the correlation oversimplification. The correct answer also embeds the keys-vs.-delegated-authority nuance specific to female auxiliary leadership, separating genuine understanding from keyword matching on 'sustain.'

question: A newly ordained elder holds the Melchizedek Priesthood, yet he cannot organize a quorum or call others to serve without direction from his quorum president. Which principle best explains this limitation?
choices: Priesthood ordination confers the authority to act, but the right to DIRECT the use of that authority is governed by priesthood keys, which are held by presiding officers
Each priesthood holder receives all keys at ordination but is asked to defer to leaders out of courtesy and good order
The elder lacks sufficient faith and worthiness; once he is fully sanctified the keys will operate through him directly
Keys are merely a symbolic teaching device; what actually restricts him is local policy in the General Handbook
source: General Handbook 3.4.1; D&C 107; Dallin H. Oaks, 'Priesthood Authority in the Family and the Church' (2005)
notes: Tests the priesthood-vs-keys distinction. Correct answer separates ordained authority from the keys that direct it. Distractor B reduces keys to etiquette; C makes it a worthiness/folk issue; D dismisses keys as symbolic. Pattern-matchers conflate 'having the priesthood' with 'having authority to direct.'

question: When a President of the Church dies, how is his successor determined according to established Church practice?
choices: The First Presidency continues governing until it selects and ordains a new President from among its members
The most senior apostle by length of ordination to the Quorum of the Twelve becomes President; the First Presidency is dissolved at the President's death
The Quorum of the Twelve nominates candidates and the apostles vote by secret ballot to elect the new President
The deceased President's first counselor automatically advances to become the new President
source: churchofjesuschrist.org, 'Succession in the Presidency'; D&C 107:22-24; recent succession of Dallin H. Oaks (Oct 2025)
notes: Tests succession mechanics. Correct: seniority by apostolic ordination + dissolution of First Presidency. Distractor C ('election by ballot') is a common anti-pattern; D ('first counselor advances') is a frequent folk misconception; A misstates timing. Seniority is by ordination to the Twelve, not age.

question: A member argues that because a stake president presides over several wards, he therefore directs the bishop in the day-to-day spiritual welfare of individual ward members. How should this be corrected doctrinally?
choices: The stake president holds all keys, so the bishop functions only as his delegate with no independent presiding authority

The bishop is the presiding high priest and common judge of his ward, holding keys for the Aaronic Priesthood and for ward members; the stake president presides over the stake but does not absorb the bishop's office
Bishops and stake presidents share identical keys, so either may act interchangeably for any ward member
The ward and stake are administrative conveniences only; spiritual presiding authority actually rests with the elders quorum president
source: General Handbook 6.1, 9.1; D&C 107:15-17, 68
notes: Tests ward-vs-stake structure and the bishop's distinct office/keys. Correct answer preserves the bishop as common judge with his own keys. A oversimplifies hierarchy into pure delegation; C falsely equates keys; D is a heterodox flattening. Requires understanding that presiding levels carry distinct, not interchangeable, keys.

question: Which statement most accurately distinguishes a priesthood QUORUM from an AUXILIARY organization such as the Relief Society or Primary?
choices: A quorum is an organized body of priesthood holders presided over by one holding keys for that quorum; an auxiliary supports and operates under the keys held by presiding priesthood leaders but is not itself a priesthood quorum
Auxiliaries possess their own independent priesthood keys equal to those of the elders quorum
Quorums and auxiliaries are identical in authority; the labels differ only by gender of the members
Auxiliaries were created by correlation in the 20th century and hold no recognized place in Church governance
source: General Handbook 4.2, 9-11; Dallin H. Oaks, 'The Keys and Authority of the Priesthood' (Apr 2014)
notes: Tests quorum/auxiliary distinction. Correct: auxiliaries function under priesthood keys, not separate keys. B grants auxiliaries independent keys (folk error); C erases the distinction; D dismisses auxiliaries. Oaks (2014) clarified women in auxiliaries exercise delegated priesthood authority under keys without holding the keys themselves.

question: In an elders quorum meeting, members raise their hands to sustain a brother called as a new quorum instructor. What does this act of sustaining most properly signify?
choices: A vote in which the majority decides whether the calling is valid
A covenant commitment to support the person and uphold the calling, exercising the law of common consent rather than electing the officer
A formal endorsement of the individual's personal worthiness, certifying he has no sins
A symbolic gesture with no governing significance, since the leader has already received the calling by revelation
source: General Handbook 3.4.3; D&C 26:2; 20:65
notes: Tests sustaining/common consent. Correct: it is covenantal support, not election. A frames it as majority rule (anti-pattern); C confuses sustaining with worthiness certification (folk error); D dismisses it as meaningless. Common consent is real governing participation without being democratic election.

question: What is the doctrinal basis for the law of common consent, by which members sustain officers and ratify Church actions?
choices: It reflects democratic governance imported from American political ideals to make the Church more participatory

It is revealed in the Doctrine and Covenants: 'all things shall be done by common consent in the church, by much prayer and faith' (D&C 26:2), so that the body ratifies, though it does not originate, callings received by revelation
It exists so that members may veto and overturn calls they personally dislike, transferring final authority to the congregation
It is a 20th-century correlation policy designed to standardize ward business meetings
source: D&C 26:2; 28:13; General Handbook 3.4.3
notes: Tests the revealed (not democratic) origin of common consent. Correct cites D&C 26:2 and the ratify-but-not-originate principle. A frames it as borrowed democracy; C inflates it into congregational veto power (Sunstone reading); D wrongly dates it to correlation. Distinguishes revelation-plus-consent from majority rule.

question: The Correlation program, strengthened under President Harold B. Lee in the 1960s–70s, is best understood as accomplishing which of the following?
choices: Placing all Church curriculum, programs, and auxiliaries under the direction of priesthood keys and a unified, doctrinally reviewed body of materials, with the family and priesthood at the center
Centralizing financial control so that local units surrender all autonomy to a corporate headquarters
Replacing revelation to local leaders with top-down bureaucratic mandates that override personal inspiration
Merging the Relief Society, Primary, and Sunday School into a single auxiliary to cut administrative costs
source: Harold B. Lee, correlation addresses (1960s); Encyclopedia of Mormonism, 'Correlation'; General Handbook 4.2
notes: Tests purpose of Correlation. Correct: aligning programs/curriculum under priesthood keys, family-centered. A reduces it to financial control (hostile spin); C frames it as suppressing revelation (Sunstone critique); D invents an auxiliary merger. Tests grasp of correlation as doctrinal-priesthood alignment, not mere bureaucracy.

question: Why does the Church emphasize councils—such as the ward council and the bishopric—rather than concentrating all decisions in a single leader?
choices: Because leaders are forbidden from acting alone and any decision made without unanimous council agreement is invalid

Because counseling together allows presiding leaders, who hold the keys and bear final responsibility, to gather inspiration and information from others before making decisions, uniting revelation with collective wisdom
Because councils operate by majority vote, the presiding officer is bound to follow whatever the council recommends
Because councils exist mainly to distribute workload, and have no role in seeking revelation
source: General Handbook 4.4; M. Russell Ballard, 'Counseling with Our Councils'; D&C 107:27-31
notes: Tests church councils. Correct: councils inform the presiding officer who retains keys and final responsibility. A overstates by requiring unanimity for validity; C makes councils binding votes (anti-pattern); D strips councils of revelatory purpose. Distinguishes counsel-then-decide from democratic decision-making.

question: Only the President of the Church may exercise all priesthood keys on the earth at one time. What is the most accurate reason given for this?
choices: Every apostle independently holds and exercises all keys at all times, so the President is merely a spokesman among equals
While all living apostles hold all the keys of the kingdom, the keys are exercised in their fulness only by the senior apostle, the President, who alone is authorized to direct their use
The President receives keys that no other apostle possesses, making the rest of the Twelve incapable of leading should he die
Keys are conferred fresh by ordinance each conference, so authority lapses if a President fails to renew them
source: D&C 132:7; Boyd K. Packer, 'The Twelve' (2008); churchofjesuschrist.org, 'Succession in the Presidency'
notes: Tests the nuanced doctrine that apostles HOLD all keys but only the President EXERCISES them fully. Correct preserves both truths, which also explains orderly succession. A flattens apostles into equals (heterodox); C claims the President holds unique keys others lack (near-miss that would break succession); D invents lapsing keys (folk error). Requires holding 'hold vs. exercise' together.

question: When a President of the Church dies, how is his successor determined according to the established pattern?
choices: The First Presidency remains intact, and the senior counselor steps up to lead the Church
The First Presidency is dissolved, and the longest-tenured (most senior) apostle in the Quorum of the Twelve becomes President
The Quorum of the Twelve and First Presidency convene to elect, by vote, the man they feel most qualified to lead
The oldest living apostle by age automatically becomes President, since age signals seniority before the Lord
source: churchofjesuschrist.org/learn/first-presidency; succession by apostolic seniority (e.g., Oaks set apart Oct 2025 as most senior apostle)
notes: Tests whether the model grasps that seniority means length of ordained service in the Twelve, not age and not counselor rank. The senior-counselor option is the natural corporate assumption (near miss); the election option imports a democratic frame foreign to the keys-based pattern; the oldest-by-age option is a common folk conflation since presidents are often elderly. Only tenure in the Quorum governs.

question: In a ward conference the bishop presents a new Relief Society president, and the congregation raises their hands to sustain her. What does this act of common consent primarily signify?
choices: A democratic election in which the majority vote of the ward confers the office upon her
A covenant of the members to uphold and support her in the calling she has received through priesthood keys and revelation
A non-binding formality acknowledging that the decision has already been finalized by the stake
An audit step in which members verify her worthiness before she may legitimately serve
source: D&C 26:2; 20:65; General Handbook 3.4.3 (common consent / sustaining)
notes: Discriminates between common consent as covenantal support versus a popular vote. The calling originates with one holding keys and is confirmed by revelation; the raised hand is the members' commitment to sustain, not the source of the authority. The 'election' option is the classic oversimplification; 'formality' under-reads its covenant weight; 'worthiness audit' confuses sustaining with the separate role of the presiding officer's interview.

question: Each member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles is ordained and given all the priesthood keys. Why, then, is the President of the Church spoken of as the only person who exercises all keys?
choices: Only the President is actually given the fulness of keys; apostles receive a lesser portion until they themselves become President
Though every apostle holds all keys, only the senior apostle—the President—is authorized to exercise them fully while he presides
The First Presidency as a body jointly exercises all keys equally, so no single man directs their use
Stake presidents and the President of the Church each exercise the full keys independently within their own jurisdictions
source: General Handbook 3.4.1; D&C 132:7; teachings on keys (e.g., Boyd K. Packer, 'The Twelve')
notes: Tests the subtle distinction between holding keys and exercising/directing them. Every apostle holds all keys, but only the presiding apostle exercises them in their fulness—which is why succession is seamless. Option A wrongly denies apostles the full keys (near miss); C flattens presiding authority into a committee (heterodox); D confuses delegated stake keys with the unique presiding authority, a common members' misunderstanding.

question: A missionary three weeks from his release date keeps steering companionship study toward stories about home and which restaurants he'll visit, and his proselyting energy has visibly flagged. Within mission vernacular, what is the precise sense in which this elder is being called 'trunky,' and how would a seasoned mission leader frame the corrective?
choices: He is 'trunky'—mentally 'packing his trunk' and disengaging near the end; leaders typically counsel him to 'die hard,' staying fully consecrated to the work until the moment of release
He is 'trunky'—suffering from homesickness common to a 'greenie,' so leaders pair him with a fresh companion to refresh his enthusiasm
He is 'trunky'—formally requesting an early release for family reasons, which the mission president must forward to Salt Lake
He is 'trunky'—being transferred to a 'trunk' area (a slow, rural region) as discipline for low baptism numbers
source: Common missionary vernacular; cf. 'greenie' (new missionary) vs. 'trunky' (preoccupied with going home); 'die hard'/'die trying' counsel
notes: Tests genuine fluency with the trunky/greenie distinction. The near-miss conflates trunky with greenie-homesickness; another invents a 'trunk area' false etymology. 'Trunky' specifically means disengagement at the end of service, and the cultural corrective is to finish strong, not an administrative process.

question: A ward member insists that because she 'prayed about it and felt a burning in the bosom,' the bishop is obligated to act on her proposal for the Primary program. From the standpoint of how personal revelation actually functions in correlated practice, what is the most doctrinally sound assessment?
choices: Personal revelation confirmed by the Spirit binds priesthood leaders, since the gift of the Holy Ghost gives every member authority over their stewardship

Personal revelation operates within the bounds of one's own stewardship; revelation for the Primary organization comes through those with keys for it, so her witness guides her own discipleship but does not direct the bishop's decisions
A 'burning in the bosom' is merely an emotional preference and has no doctrinal standing; only the bishop receives any revelation in the ward
Because the bishop holds keys, members are discouraged from seeking personal revelation about ward matters at all, to avoid competing impressions
source: D&C 9:8–9; principle that revelation follows lines of stewardship/keys; Oaks, 'Two Lines of Communication'
notes: Tests the stewardship boundary of personal revelation—a subtle point. Distractors over-extend revelation to override keys (progressive), dismiss spiritual confirmation as mere emotion (anti), or forbid personal revelation entirely (oversimplification). The key idea is revelation-within-stewardship, not a trump card over priesthood keys.

question: A new bishop is about to be installed. A well-meaning member explains the process to a recent convert. Which description most accurately reflects how a bishop is actually called, set apart, and sustained?
choices: The ward nominates candidates and votes by secret ballot; the winner is forwarded to the stake president for approval

The stake president, after seeking inspiration (and First Presidency approval of the recommendation), extends the call; the ward then sustains him by common consent, and he is ordained/set apart—he is not elected
The outgoing bishop selects his own successor, who is then ratified by the high council
The Quorum of the Twelve calls each bishop directly by revelation, bypassing local leaders to ensure impartiality
source: General Handbook 7.1; bishops called by stake president with First Presidency approval, sustained by common consent
notes: Tests understanding that 'sustaining' is common consent, not election, and that the stake president (with FP approval) calls the bishop. Distractors include the democratic-vote misconception, a folk idea that bishops hand-pick successors, and an over-centralized near-miss.

question: In the temple-recommend renewal process under current practice (post-2019 revisions), which statement best captures how worthiness is actually assessed and certified?
choices: A single interview with the bishop suffices, since he is the common judge and stake involvement was eliminated in the 2019 revisions
Two interviews—one with a member of the bishopric and one with a member of the stake presidency—certify worthiness; the 2019 changes clarified wording but did not lower the worthiness standards
The bishop administers a written questionnaire scored against a numeric threshold; those above the cutoff receive a recommend
Because the 2019 revisions emphasized grace, the questions now focus on belief alone and no longer ask about behavioral standards like the Word of Wisdom or tithing
source: Temple recommend questions revised Oct 2019; two-interview process (bishopric + stake presidency); worthiness standards unchanged
notes: Tests fluency with the actual two-interview structure and the fact that 2019 changes were verbiage clarifications, not relaxed standards. Distractors drop the stake interview, invent a scoring scheme, and push a grace-only revisionist read.

question: At BYU, a returned-missionary student tells his roommate he's anxious about 'ring by spring.' A faculty member overhears and wants to contextualize the phrase accurately rather than reinforce a stereotype. Which framing is most accurate to the actual culture and to Church teaching on marriage?
choices: 'Ring by spring' is an official BYU graduation requirement that students be engaged before their senior year

'Ring by spring' is a tongue-in-cheek cultural quip about the high pace of dating-to-engagement at BYU; while Church leaders encourage marriage, the doctrine emphasizes not rushing into it unwisely but seeking it prayerfully and deliberately
'Ring by spring' reflects a binding doctrine that delaying marriage past one's early twenties is sinful, enforced through the Honor Code
'Ring by spring' is anti-Mormon mockery with no basis in actual BYU student culture
source: BYU dating culture vernacular; leaders encourage marriage as a priority while counseling wise, prayerful choice (cf. counsel against both delaying unduly and marrying hastily)
notes: Tests ability to separate genuine cultural humor from official policy and folk legalism. Distractors falsely institutionalize the phrase, turn it into a sin-doctrine, or dismiss it as fabricated. The nuance: real cultural phenomenon + measured doctrinal encouragement, neither requirement nor sin.

question: A recently baptized convert is overwhelmed when given a calling to teach Primary within two months. An experienced ward council member explains the principle behind extending callings to new converts. Which reasoning best reflects sound practice in convert integration?
choices: New converts should receive no callings until they have been members at least one year, to ensure doctrinal maturity

Meaningful callings help converts feel needed, build friendships, and grow through service ('a friend, a responsibility, and nurturing by the word'); leaders match the calling to readiness rather than withholding service entirely
Converts must be given the most demanding callings immediately to test the sincerity of their conversion
Callings for converts are purely about filling vacancies; spiritual development is irrelevant to how assignments are made
source: President Gordon B. Hinckley's counsel that every convert needs 'a friend, a responsibility, and nurturing by the good word of God'
notes: Tests convert-integration practice. The folk-doctrine distractor invents a one-year waiting rule; others distort callings into a loyalty test or mere staffing. The Hinckley 'friend/responsibility/nurturing' framework is the correlated standard, with leaders calibrating to readiness.

question: Two missionaries debate how to observe P-day. One argues it is simply 'a day off' to do whatever they want; the other says it has a defined purpose. Which best describes the actual nature and limits of preparation day in mission culture?
choices: P-day is a full day of liberty with no missionary rules in effect, since missionaries need complete rest

P-day ('preparation day') is a weekly day for tasks like laundry, shopping, letters, and wholesome recreation; missionary standards, companionship rules, and some proselyting still apply, and it is not a license to set aside one's purpose
P-day stands for 'proselyting day,' the one day each week missionaries are permitted to knock doors
P-day is determined individually by each missionary's mood and can be taken on any day they feel unmotivated
source: Missionary Handbook: preparation day for personal tasks and wholesome recreation; mission rules and standards remain in force
notes: Tests precise understanding of P-day's purpose and limits. Distractors treat it as a rules-free day off, misexpand the acronym to 'proselyting day,' or invent mood-based scheduling. The key: a structured preparation day where missionary standards still apply.

question: At a transfer meeting, a missionary jokes that his new companion is a 'greenie.' What does that mean?
choices: A missionary who is newly arrived in the field and just out of the MTC
A missionary who is counting down the days until he goes home
A missionary serving in a rural, outdoors-heavy area
A missionary who has been disciplined and is on probation
source: Mission vernacular; Preach My Gospel culture
notes: 'Greenie' = brand-new missionary. Distractor B is 'trunky' (near-miss on a different real term), C invents a folk meaning, D is a hostile spin. Tests fluency in core mission slang, not pattern-matching the word 'green.'

question: A missionary describes himself as 'trunky' in his final weeks. What is he expressing?
choices: That he is mentally checked out, focused on going home rather than the work
That he has packed all his belongings and is ready to be transferred
That he is feeling spiritually burned out and discouraged
That he has been assigned to drive the mission vehicle
source: Mission vernacular ('trunky' from packing one's trunk to go home)
notes: 'Trunky' = preoccupied with going home near the end of a mission. B and C are believable near-misses tied to the word's imagery; D is invented. Tests understanding of the term's emotional meaning.

question: When a member says, 'I prayed about it and felt good, so I'm taking the job,' what cultural concept are they invoking?
choices: Seeking personal revelation and a spiritual confirmation for a personal decision
Asking the bishop's permission before making a major life choice
A guarantee that the outcome will be financially successful
Following a folk superstition rather than any real Church teaching
source: D&C 9 ('burning in the bosom'); personal revelation teachings
notes: This frames decisions as seeking personal revelation/confirmation. B oversimplifies authority structure, C is a prosperity misreading, D is hostile dismissal. Tests understanding of how members talk about confirmation, not mere preference.

question: What does the BYU phrase 'ring by spring' refer to?
choices: The cultural expectation that many students will get engaged during the school year
An honor-code rule requiring married students to wear wedding bands
A springtime devotional series about temple marriage
A scholarship awarded to engaged students
source: BYU campus culture; high marriage-rate vernacular
notes: 'Ring by spring' is a lighthearted nod to the campus marriage culture, not a rule. B turns it into a false Honor Code item, C and D invent programs/perks. Tests cultural fluency vs. literalizing the phrase.

question: A new convert is baptized on Saturday. Which best reflects how the ward typically integrates them afterward?
choices: Confirmation, then receiving a calling and ministering companions to help them stay engaged
They must wait one year before participating in any ward responsibilities
They are immediately ordained a high priest to ensure full activity
Integration is left entirely to the missionaries, not the ward
source: General Handbook on convert retention; ministering
notes: Converts are confirmed and quickly given a calling and ministering support. B invents a waiting period, C wildly overstates ordination, D wrongly offloads to missionaries. Tests how retention actually works at the ward level.

question: How does an active adult member obtain a temple recommend?
choices: Through two worthiness interviews—one with a member of the bishopric and one with the stake presidency
By paying a one-time temple admission fee at the temple desk
By passing a written doctrinal exam administered by the ward clerk
Automatically, once they have been a member for one year
source: Temple recommend interview practice (bishop + stake presidency)
notes: Two interviews certify worthiness. B implies pay-to-enter (hostile/false), C invents an exam, D invents an automatic timeline. Tests lived practice of the recommend process.

question: In a ward, what is a 'calling'?
choices: An assignment to serve in a Church position, extended by leaders and accepted by faith
A paid staff position one applies and interviews for
A personal spiritual prompting to choose one's own ministry
A temporary task that ends after a single Sunday
source: General Handbook; lay service callings
notes: Callings are assignments accepted by faith, not jobs or self-selected ministries. B is the professional-clergy model, C confuses calling with personal revelation, D trivializes duration. Tests understanding of lay service.

question: A 15-year-old wakes early each weekday before school for 'seminary.' What is this?
choices: A daily scripture-study religious education class for youth ages roughly 14–18
The two-week training all youth complete before serving a mission
A program preparing teens to become professional clergy
A weekend youth camp held once per year
source: Seminary & Institute program for youth
notes: Seminary is daily youth religious instruction (often early-morning). B confuses it with the MTC, C imports the Protestant 'seminary = clergy training' meaning, D invents a camp. Tests fluency in youth programs vs. the word's other-faith meaning.

question: In a typical ward, how does a man become the bishop?
choices: The ward members nominate candidates and vote in a congregational election, and the winner is ordained.
He is called by the stake president through inspiration, then presented to the ward to be sustained, and serves as an unpaid lay leader.
He applies to Church headquarters, completes seminary-style clergy training, and is hired to a salaried pastoral position.
The outgoing bishop personally chooses his own successor and ordains him before being released.
source: General Handbook 30.7; cultural-fluency anchor: a bishop is called by the stake president through inspiration and sustained (not elected) by the ward, serving as unpaid lay clergy
notes: Tests whether the model grasps the call-and-sustain pattern versus democratic or professional-clergy models. The 'election' option is a progressive/congregationalist trap (sustaining is common consent, NOT a vote among rival candidates); the 'salaried, trained, hired pastor' option is an anti-pattern importing paid-clergy assumptions foreign to the lay ministry; the 'outgoing bishop picks his successor' is a plausible near-miss that gets the right players (a priesthood leader extends the call) but the wrong authority and direction (it is the stake president, with First Presidency approval, not the previous bishop). Only the keyed answer captures both the inspired call from the stake president and sustaining by common consent.

question: A new bishop is announced in sacrament meeting and the ward is invited to raise hands to sustain. A recent convert asks what that raised hand actually means. Which response best captures the Latter-day Saint principle at work?
choices: The raised hand is a democratic vote electing the bishop; had a majority voted against him, the ward would nominate another candidate.
The bishop was called by the stake president through inspiration and approved by the First Presidency; the raised hand is a covenant of common consent to uphold and support him, not an election.
Sustaining is a courtesy that merely acknowledges the announcement and creates no real obligation, since the calling is a purely administrative appointment.
The congregation's vote ratifies a name that the ward council first nominated and forwarded to the stake president for approval.
source: General Handbook 30.6 (calling a bishop); D&C 20:65; 26:2 (common consent)
notes: Tests whether the model grasps that 'sustaining' is consent-by-covenant under priesthood keys, not democratic election (A oversimplifies the show of hands into a vote) and not a hollow formality (C empties common consent of its binding nature). D appears procedurally plausible but inverts the order—bishops are called top-down by the stake president with First Presidency approval, never nominated by ward council. Distinguishes understanding of common consent from pattern-matched 'voting' language.

question: An elders quorum president, after sincere prayer, feels strongly that a particular sister should be called to serve in Primary, and tells the bishop he has 'received revelation' about it. Considering how personal revelation and stewardship interrelate, what is the most doctrinally sound assessment?
choices: Because he received a genuine spiritual confirmation, the bishop should act on it; true personal revelation overrides organizational lines of authority.

Personal revelation is real, but it operates within the bounds of one's stewardship; calling sisters to Primary lies under the bishop's keys, so the impression is at most counsel to be weighed—not directive revelation binding on the bishop.
Revelation for other people is impossible; the Spirit only ever confirms decisions about oneself, so the impression should simply be disregarded.
Such impressions are personal preference dressed in spiritual language and should be treated with suspicion as incipient unrighteous dominion.
source: D&C 28:2-7 (Hiram Page episode); Oaks, 'Two Lines of Communication,' Oct 2010; General Handbook 4.2.4-5
notes: Tests the keys/stewardship boundary on personal revelation. A is the common folk overreach (a sincere impression trumps authority)—precisely the error D&C 28 corrects. C overcorrects into a false absolute (one can receive promptings to bless others, just not to direct another's stewardship). D dismisses revelation entirely as a power grab (Sunstone-flavored). Only B holds both truths: revelation is real AND channeled by keys.

question: A devoted member preparing for her temple recommend interview hesitates, fearing she is not 'worthy' because she still wrestles with occasional impatience and sincere doubts. Which best reflects how worthiness actually functions in temple-recommend practice?
choices: Worthiness requires being free of sin and doubt at the moment of the interview; any unresolved weakness disqualifies a person until it is fully conquered.

Worthiness concerns the direction of one's life—honest repentance, keeping covenants, and faith in Christ—rather than flawless perfection; ordinary weaknesses and sincere questions do not, by themselves, bar a recommend.
Since salvation is by grace alone, worthiness is beside the point; the interview merely confirms membership and that tithing is paid.
Worthiness is ultimately self-certified—the questions are private matters of conscience, so the interviewer has no standing to withhold a recommend.
source: General Handbook 26.3; temple recommend questions (rev. Oct 2019); Holland, 'Tomorrow the Lord Will Do Wonders Among You,' Apr 2016
notes: Tests the lived meaning of worthiness as trajectory/repentance rather than sinless perfection. A is the works-righteousness oversimplification that drives needless scrupulosity. C imports the grace-alone (protestant) frame that makes worthiness irrelevant—false in LDS theology where covenants and the interview matter. D is the heterodox 'no one can judge me' reading that erases the interviewer's keys. Discriminates models that understand striving-discipleship from those defaulting to either legalism or grace-alone.

question: In missionary slang, an elder with three weeks left who keeps talking about cars, food, and seeing his family is described as 'trunky.' What does the term communicate?
choices: He is spiritually seasoned and ready to 'graduate' into post-mission leadership
He is mentally 'packing his trunk' — distracted by going home and losing focus on the work
He is newly arrived and still overwhelmed by the missionary routine
He is simply homesick, which is treated the same as any new missionary's adjustment
source: Common missionary vernacular; cf. missionary culture anchors (RM, greenie, trunky, transfers, P-day)
notes: 'Trunky' = mentally checked-out near release ('packing the trunk'). Distractor C is the opposite term ('greenie'); A inverts the meaning into something positive; D flattens it into mere homesickness. Tests whether a model knows the disapproving, focus-losing connotation rather than just 'wants to go home.'

question: A BYU student wants to stay within the Honor Code's Word-of-Wisdom standard. Which choice is actually acceptable?
choices: A decaffeinated coffee, since removing the caffeine makes it permissible
A caffeinated cola soft drink with lunch
An iced latte, since the prohibition only covers drinks served hot
Green tea, because only black tea counts as a forbidden 'hot drink'
source: D&C 89; Newsroom 'Statement on the Word of Wisdom' (Aug 2019); BYU Honor Code
notes: The prohibition targets coffee and tea (the tea plant) — not caffeine per se and not temperature. Caffeinated soda is not banned. A and C reveal the caffeine/temperature folk misunderstandings; D is a near-miss (green AND black tea both come from the tea plant). Tests grasp of WHY, not keyword 'caffeine.'

question: How does a man become bishop of a ward, and what does the ward's 'sustaining vote' actually mean?
choices: The ward elects him by majority vote, and the raised hands are the ballots
An area seventy appoints him to a salaried clergy position over the congregation
The stake president calls him through inspiration and he is ordained; the ward then 'sustains' him as a covenant to support, not a popular election
He volunteers for the post and is approved by the Quorum of the Twelve
source: General Handbook; cultural-fluency anchor on how a bishop is called and sustained
notes: A bishop is a lay, unpaid leader called by the stake president by revelation, then sustained. The 'sustaining' is a commitment to support, not a democratic election (A's misconception). B injects paid clergy/wrong authority; D wrongly puts the Twelve in a local call. Tests the call-and-sustain distinction.

question: After three years as Primary president, Sister Alvarez is 'released' in sacrament meeting. What does being released signify?
choices: She was found unworthy and is being quietly disciplined before the ward
Her temporary assignment has honorably ended; callings rotate and members move to new ones
She is permanently barred from holding any calling in the future
She quit because she disliked the work and asked to be let go
source: General Handbook; ward dynamics / callings in practice
notes: Releases are routine and honorable; callings are temporary lay assignments that rotate. A is the hostile 'punishment' spin; C overstates permanence; D assumes the member's preference drove it. Tests understanding that release ≠ discipline or personal choice.

question: At BYU, students joke about getting a 'ring by spring.' What does the phrase reflect?
choices: A doctrine requiring students to marry before they may graduate
A tongue-in-cheek cultural expectation of engagement during the school year — reflecting the Church's emphasis on marriage, but not a commandment or rule
A temple ordinance performed for engaged students each spring semester
A traditional send-off for missionaries departing in the spring
source: BYU campus culture; emphasis on eternal marriage (Family Proclamation, 1995)
notes: 'Ring by spring' is cultural humor about early engagement, rooted in genuine marriage emphasis but carrying no doctrinal force. A inflates it into a requirement; C and D invent ordinances/traditions. Tests ability to separate lived cultural pressure from doctrine.

question: A member weighing a job offer says, 'I studied it out, prayed about it, and felt at peace.' What does this best reflect in Latter-day Saint practice?
choices: The belief that any peaceful feeling is an infallible command that overrides one's own study and judgment
Seeking personal revelation to confirm a decision one has reasoned through — 'study it out in your mind,' then a confirming peace or 'burning in the bosom' (D&C 9)
An acknowledgment that the bishop actually made the decision on the member's behalf
A claim to prophetic authority that is binding on other people
source: D&C 9:7–9; cultural-fluency anchor on personal revelation
notes: The pattern is study + decision + prayerful confirmation, not feelings replacing thought. A is the oversimplified 'feelings are infallible' version; C and D misplace the authority. Tests grasp of the D&C 9 'study it out' model versus pure emotion or outsourced decisions.

question: How does an adult member obtain or renew a temple recommend?
choices: A single interview conducted by the temple president at the temple entrance
Two worthiness interviews — one with a member of the bishopric and one with a member of the stake presidency — with periodic renewal
Payment of an entrance fee at the temple recommend desk on arrival
Self-certifying worthiness through an online portal without an interview
source: General Handbook; temple recommend interview practice (questions revised Oct 2019)
notes: A recommend requires two interviews (bishopric + stake presidency) and periodic renewal — not a temple-desk transaction. C is the hostile 'pay to enter' spin; A and D are near-misses on who interviews and how. Tests the actual two-interview, lay-clergy worthiness process.

question: President Gordon B. Hinckley taught that every new convert needs three things to stay rooted in the Church. Which set captures his counsel?
choices: A friend, a responsibility (a calling or assignment), and to be 'nourished by the good word of God'
An immediate temple endowment, a mission call, and full tithing within the first year
To memorize the Articles of Faith, attend BYU, and be sealed in the temple within twelve months
A monthly check-in quota and a formal probationary membership period
source: Gordon B. Hinckley, 'Converts and Young Men,' Apr 1997 (Moroni 6:4)
notes: The three needs are a friend, a responsibility, and nurturing by the word of God — low-pressure integration. B front-loads ordinances/obligations; C is a cultural-checklist fantasy; D invents a probationary status that doesn't exist. Tests knowledge of convert retention principles.

question: A 15-year-old member mentions she goes to 'seminary' before school each morning. What is seminary?
choices: A training program reserved for youth preparing to serve full-time missions
The Missionary Training Center, where new missionaries learn before their assignments
A four-year religious-education program for high-school-age youth (roughly grades 9–12), often early-morning or released-time, studying the standard works on a rotating annual schedule
The weekly midweek activity night that replaced the Church's Scouting program
source: Seminary and Institute of Religion program; Come, Follow Me / standard-works rotation
notes: Seminary is daily scripture study for teens, not mission prep or the MTC, and is distinct from weeknight youth activities. A and B confuse it with missionary structures; D conflates it with the Children and Youth activity program. Tests basic literacy about youth religious education.

question: An elder with three weeks left on his mission keeps talking about his college plans, has stopped studying with intensity, and seems mentally checked out. His companion jokingly tells him to stop being so 'trunky.' What does this missionary vernacular convey?
choices: He is preoccupied with going home — emotionally 'packing his trunk' — and has lost focus on the work
He is a brand-new missionary still learning the ropes and making rookie mistakes
He is refusing to follow mission rules and is at risk of being sent home early for disobedience
He is homesick in a clinical sense and should be referred to a mission mental-health counselor
source: Common missionary vernacular; cf. Church mission culture (RM, greenie, transfers, P-day)
notes: Tests lived mission fluency. 'Trunky' = preoccupied with going home near the end of one's mission (the new missionary term is 'greenie,' the near-miss distractor). It is not a disciplinary or clinical term; conflating it with those reflects pattern-matching rather than cultural literacy.

question: A ward's beloved bishop is released after about five years, and members wonder how the next one is chosen. Which description best matches actual Church practice?
choices: The stake president, after seeking inspiration (with First Presidency approval), extends the call; the ward then sustains the new bishop by common consent
The ward members nominate and vote among candidates, and the man with the most votes is ordained bishop
An Area Seventy interviews the ward and appoints the most spiritually qualified man as a paid local pastor
The outgoing bishop personally selects and ordains his own successor before being released
source: General Handbook 6.3; Articles of Faith 5; law of common consent (D&C 26:2)
notes: Tests understanding that callings come by inspiration and authority from above, then are 'sustained' (not elected) — the sustaining is ratification, not a vote. Distractors swap in congregational democracy, a paid clergy/appointment model, and self-succession, each plausible to outsiders but contrary to practice.

question: A young woman tells her roommate, 'I prayed about whether to accept his proposal, and I just felt at peace, so I said yes.' Within Latter-day Saint culture, what is she primarily claiming?
choices: That she sought and received personal revelation — a spiritual confirmation — rather than deciding on preference alone
That God has revealed this is her one predestined soulmate and no other choice was ever possible
That she felt no obligation to study it out herself, since the peaceful feeling settled everything instantly
That her bishop and stake president must now ratify the engagement before it can proceed
source: D&C 9:7–9 ('study it out in your mind'); personal revelation as confirmation
notes: Tests grasp of how 'I prayed about it' frames decisions as seeking divine confirmation, not mere feeling. The 'one soulmate' option is classic folk doctrine the Church does not teach; the 'no study needed' option ignores the D&C 9 pattern of study-then-confirm; leaders do not ratify personal marriage choices.

question: A recently baptized convert wants to attend the temple to be baptized for deceased relatives. What does the standard temple-recommend process actually require of her?
choices: A worthiness interview with both a member of the bishopric and a member of the stake presidency for a recommend; typically she waits about a year before receiving her own endowment
A single interview with the bishop, after which she may immediately receive her own endowment and be sealed
A perfect record of never having broken the Word of Wisdom or law of chastity in her entire life
Approval voted on by the ward council, since temple attendance is a congregational privilege
source: General Handbook 26.3; temple recommend interviews (bishop + stake presidency); typical one-year wait for endowment
notes: Tests practical literacy: a limited-use recommend for baptisms for the dead still involves two-level interviews, and new converts customarily wait about a year for the endowment. Distractors exploit the misconception of a single interview, a 'sinless perfection' standard (the recommend assesses current worthiness/repentance, not a flawless past), and a congregational-vote model.

question: In Latter-day Saint theology, what is the precise relationship between 'intelligence' (D&C 93:29) and the premortal 'spirits' or 'intelligences' (Abraham 3:22)?
choices: Intelligence and spirit are synonyms: God created spirits ex nihilo at the beginning of the premortal realm
The eternal, uncreated intelligence (light of truth) was at some point organized into spirit bodies as spirit children of God, so the spirit had a beginning the underlying intelligence did not
Intelligences are unembodied divine ideas in the mind of God that only become real upon mortal birth
God organized eternal matter into spirits but Himself created the intelligence within them
source: D&C 93:29, 33; Abraham 3:18, 22; King Follett Discourse
notes: The fine point that separates faculty-level understanding: 'intelligence/light of truth' is uncreated and co-eternal (D&C 93:29 'neither indeed can be' created), while the spirit child is an organization of that intelligence (spirit birth). A asserts ex nihilo creation (protestant_trap, also denies co-eternity). C is a heterodox Platonic reading. D concedes uncreated matter but wrongly has God creating the intelligence itself, contradicting D&C 93:29.

question: How does mainstream Latter-day Saint soteriology read the phrase 'it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do' (2 Nephi 25:23)?
choices: Grace activates only once a person has earned it by maxing out personal righteousness; works are the cause and grace the reward
Salvation is by grace alone through faith; the works clause is a corruption later inserted into the text

Grace is the necessary and sufficient cause of salvation; 'after all we can do' denotes logical separateness (grace applies apart from our works) and the ongoing covenant of discipleship, not a wage earned by exhausting effort first
Humans are saved by grace for resurrection but must earn exaltation entirely by their own merits without further grace
source: 2 Nephi 25:23; Moroni 10:32; 'True to the Faith' (Grace); Bednar/Robinson on 'after = separation'
notes: Advanced soteriology. The official position (cf. True to the Faith, Stephen Robinson, Brad Wilcox) reads 'after' as separation not strict temporal sequence: grace is primary, but covenant effort matters. A is the common works-righteousness caricature members and critics both assume (correlation_oversimplification). B is the Protestant grace-alone reading plus a CES-style textual claim. D is a widespread folk bifurcation that wrongly walls grace out of exaltation, contradicting Moroni 10:32 ('by his grace ye may be perfect').

question: Lehi teaches that 'Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy' (2 Nephi 2:25). What does this verse establish about the Fall in Latter-day Saint doctrine?
choices: The Fall was a tragic accident that frustrated God's plan and is the reason mortality is fundamentally evil
The Fall was a foreseen, necessary, and ultimately positive transgression that introduced mortality, agency, and the conditions for human progression and joy
Adam and Eve inherited a depraved nature transmitted to all humanity, who are therefore born guilty of original sin
The Fall was purely symbolic; there was no literal Adam, so the doctrine teaches only that humanity is morally imperfect
source: 2 Nephi 2:22-25; Moses 5:10-11; Articles of Faith 1:2
notes: Tests the distinctively LDS 'felix culpa' theology: the Fall was a 'fall forward,' necessary and good, not catastrophe. A is a fallen-world pessimism foreign to LDS thought. C is Augustinian/Reformed original sin and inherited guilt, explicitly rejected by AoF 1:2 ('men will be punished for their own sins'). D is a heterodox non-literal reading. The correct answer captures Eve's later rejoicing (Moses 5:11) and the necessity of opposition (2 Ne 2:11).

question: D&C 76 describes those who inherit the telestial glory. What is doctrinally distinctive about the telestial kingdom relative to common assumptions?
choices: It is essentially equivalent to outer darkness, a place of unending torment for the wicked
Although the lowest of the three degrees of glory, its glory 'surpasses all understanding' (D&C 76:89), and its inheritors are still redeemed from spiritual death after suffering for their sins
It is a temporary holding state from which all eventually progress upward into the celestial kingdom
Only sons of perdition are assigned there, having denied the Holy Ghost after receiving it
notes: Advanced eschatology. Even the lowest glory is glorious 'beyond understanding' (76:89) and its heirs are saved (not damned) after paying for their sins in the postmortal spirit world. A conflates telestial with outer darkness (anti_mormon caricature of 'low heaven = hell'). C is the popular but officially-unsanctioned 'eternal progression between kingdoms' folk doctrine (Church leaders have declined to endorse it). D misidentifies the telestial heirs as sons of perdition (who receive no glory).

question: The Book of Abraham presents the 'Gnolaum' / eternal nature of spirits and the council in heaven (Abraham 3). What does Abraham 3:22-28 add to the doctrine of the premortal council that is not found as explicitly elsewhere in the standard works?
choices: It identifies Kolob as the planet on which God physically resides and governs the universe

It depicts the noble and great ones chosen as premortal leaders, and frames the plan as a question ('Whom shall I send?') answered by two responding parties, with the Beloved's plan accepted and the second's rebellion
It teaches that all spirits are equal in capacity in the premortal world, with mortal differences arising only from environment
It establishes that the war in heaven was fought over whether God should have a physical body
source: Abraham 3:22-28; Moses 4:1-4
notes: Pearl of Great Price item. Abraham 3 uniquely records foreordination of 'noble and great ones' and the council scene with two responders (the Beloved Son vs. Lucifer). A is the pervasive folk reading of Kolob (Abr 3:3 calls it nearest to God's throne, NOT His residence). C is an egalitarian heterodox gloss contradicting the foreordination of differing capacities (Abr 3:18-19, 22). D mistakes the actual issue of the war (agency vs. compulsion, Moses 4:1-3), not embodiment.

question: Latter-day Saints affirm the Godhead as three distinct beings. How should the relationship between the Father and the Son in passages like Mosiah 15:1-5 ('the Father, because he was conceived by the power of God; and the Son, because of the flesh') be understood within official doctrine?
choices: Mosiah 15 proves the Father and Son are the same person under different titles (modalism), which is the correct LDS view

Abinadi uses 'Father' and 'Son' titles to describe Christ's roles (Father by divine investiture of authority and as Creator/Father of our salvation, Son in the flesh); this does NOT collapse the Father and Son into one being, who remain separate and distinct
The Book of Mormon here contradicts the later First Vision, showing the doctrine of God evolved from one being to three
Jesus literally became His own father by a process of eternal regression
source: Mosiah 15:1-5; D&C 130:22; 'The Father and the Son' (1916 First Presidency doctrinal exposition)
notes: This is a classic apparent-contradiction passage that separates real understanding from pattern-matching. The 1916 First Presidency exposition resolves it: Christ is called 'Father' by divine investiture of authority and as Creator/Father of the faithful, not because He is the same person as Elohim. A is modalism (protestant_trap, a oneness/Sabellian error). C is the CES-Letter 'evolving God' argument (anti_mormon_trap). D is a confused folk extrapolation.

question: D&C 130:22-23 specifies the physical nature of the Godhead. Which statement most precisely reflects the doctrine, including its historical development in Joseph Smith's teaching?
choices: All three members of the Godhead possess tangible bodies of flesh and bone, which is why the Holy Ghost can dwell in our hearts
The Father and the Son have bodies of flesh and bone as tangible as man's; the Holy Ghost is a personage of spirit, which makes possible His indwelling influence
The Father is a spirit only, while the Son took on flesh; the Holy Ghost is an impersonal force
The Godhead shares one substance (homoousios) expressed in three persons, consistent with the Nicene Creed
source: D&C 130:22-23; Lectures on Faith 5 (and its later superseding)
notes: Precise embodiment doctrine. The Father and Son are embodied; the Holy Ghost is deliberately a spirit personage so He can indwell. A is a common members' overstatement giving the Holy Ghost a body (folk_doctrine_trap) and misreasons the indwelling. C strips the Father of a body (echoes the earlier Lectures on Faith 5 view that was later superseded by D&C 130, a progressive/dated reading). D is the Nicene homoousios (protestant_trap), explicitly rejected.

question: How does Latter-day Saint doctrine characterize the Great Apostasy and the resulting need for a Restoration, as opposed to a Reformation?
choices: The Church merely became corrupt in practice while retaining valid priesthood authority, so reform from within (as the Reformers attempted) was sufficient

Priesthood authority and saving ordinances were lost from the earth through apostasy, so a restoration by heavenly messengers conferring keys anew was required, not a reform of an existing valid church
Truth was never lost; the Restoration simply re-emphasized neglected biblical teachings already present in mainstream Christianity
The apostasy affected only the Eastern churches, while Roman Catholicism preserved unbroken priesthood authority that Joseph Smith inherited
source: D&C 1:30; D&C 27:12-13; Joseph Smith—History 1:19; Restoration Proclamation (2020); 2 Thessalonians 2:3
notes: Restoration item testing the restoration-not-reformation distinction. The key claim is loss of priesthood authority/keys requiring angelic restoration (JS-H 1:72; D&C 13, 27). A wrongly grants surviving valid authority needing only reform (the Protestant rationale the Restoration explicitly rejects). C is an ecumenical/progressive softening that denies any real apostasy. D invents an unbroken-Catholic-line claim foreign to LDS doctrine (plausible_near_miss).

question: In the plan of salvation, what is the doctrinal status and source of moral agency, and how does it relate to the existence of opposition and law (2 Nephi 2; D&C 93)?
choices: Agency was granted to humans at mortal birth by God as a revocable gift, and could in principle be taken back

Agency is rooted in the eternal, self-existent intelligence of man; God did not create it from nothing, and its meaningful exercise requires opposition, law, and the capacity to act and not merely be acted upon
Agency means humans are entirely autonomous and unaccountable, since God foreknows but does not foreordain
Agency is libertarian freedom unconstrained by any law, so consequences are arbitrary rather than fixed
notes: Advanced item linking agency to the eternal nature of intelligence and to fixed law. Because intelligence is uncreated, agency is intrinsic, not a bestowed-and-revocable gift (A, plausible_near_miss). The exercise of agency presupposes opposition and law (2 Ne 2:11-13) and irrevocably decreed law-blessing pairings (D&C 130:20-21), refuting the 'no law/arbitrary' view (D, folk libertarianism). C is a heterodox denial of accountability and foreordination.

question: The Three Nephites (3 Nephi 28), John the Beloved (D&C 7), and the city of Enoch (Moses 7) are all described as 'translated.' Which statement most precisely captures the doctrine of translation as distinct from both mortality and resurrection?
choices: Translation is simply a poetic word for being resurrected early, so translated beings already possess glorified, immortal bodies of flesh and bone
Translated beings are taken directly to the celestial kingdom and exalted, bypassing death, judgment, and the resurrection entirely

Translation is a changed mortal state in which the body is sanctified so as not to taste death or feel pain and Satan has no power over them, but they have not yet been resurrected and must still be changed 'in the twinkling of an eye' from mortality to immortality at Christ's coming
Translation means the spirit is taken from the body to dwell in paradise while the body sleeps, exactly as with any other righteous person who dies
source: 3 Nephi 28:7-9, 36-40; D&C 7:1-3; Moses 7:21, 63-69; Joseph Smith, Teachings (translated beings held in terrestrial order)
notes: A equates translation with resurrection, granting an immortal glorified body now (plausible_near_miss) — but 3 Ne 28:8 says they will yet be changed to immortality at the Second Coming, so they are not yet resurrected. B is the folk leap that translation = instant exaltation, skipping judgment and resurrection (folk_doctrine_trap). D collapses translation into ordinary death (spirit leaves a sleeping body), erasing the whole point that translated beings do NOT taste death (plausible_near_miss). C is correct: a changed-but-still-mortal terrestrial-order state, awaiting the resurrection change. Tests the precise three-way distinction among mortality, translation, and resurrection that students routinely conflate.

question: In Ether 3 the brother of Jared sees the finger, then the full body, of the premortal Lord. What does this episode teach about the nature of Christ's premortal spirit and His identity, according to the text and mainstream Latter-day Saint reading?
choices: The being who appeared was God the Father, Elohim, showing that the Father and the Son are the same personage under different names
Christ appeared in His resurrected body of flesh and bone, demonstrating that He already possessed a physical body before Bethlehem

Christ showed the body of His spirit — which has the form and appearance of flesh and blood though it is spirit — and identified Himself as Jehovah/Jesus Christ, the premortal Redeemer in whose spirit image man was created
The 'body' the brother of Jared saw was only a symbolic vision with no claim about the actual form of spirits, since spirits in LDS doctrine are formless light
source: Ether 3:6-16; Mosiah 3:5; The Father and the Son: A Doctrinal Exposition (1916)
notes: A reads the appearance modalistically as the Father and collapses Father and Son into one personage (protestant_trap / modalism, which LDS doctrine rejects). B claims a premortal body of flesh and bone, but Ether 3:16 has Christ call it 'the body of my spirit,' not yet incarnate flesh (plausible_near_miss). D denies spirits any form, contradicting D&C 131:7-8 and Ether 3 where the spirit body appears in human form (folk_doctrine_trap). C is correct: the premortal Jehovah (Jesus, not the Father) shows His spirit body, which has the appearance of flesh and blood and is the pattern for man's creation. Tests both the spirit-has-form doctrine and the Jehovah=Son identification, against modalism and against a premature 'physical body.'

question: Book of Mormon prophets (2 Nephi 9, Alma 12, Helaman 14) teach that the Fall brought TWO deaths and that the Atonement and Resurrection answer each differently. Which statement most accurately states this two-deaths soteriology?
choices: There is only one death — the separation of body and spirit — and the Resurrection unconditionally overcomes it, after which all are judged solely by works

The Atonement overcomes temporal death (body/spirit separation) UNCONDITIONALLY through universal resurrection, while the SPIRITUAL death (separation from God) is overcome CONDITIONALLY through repentance and faith — though the resurrection first redeems all from the initial spiritual death brought by the Fall so they may be brought back into God's presence to be judged
Both the first and second deaths are overcome unconditionally for everyone, so that no soul finally remains separated from God's presence
Spiritual death is the only real death that matters; physical death is an illusion, and the body is never literally reunited with the spirit
notes: A reduces the two deaths to one and makes judgment works-only, ignoring the conditional dimension of spiritual death (correlation_oversimplification). C is universalism in which the second/spiritual death is overcome for all, contradicting Helaman 14:18 and Alma 12 where the second death (final separation) falls on the unrepentant (progressive_trap). D denies the literal bodily resurrection, a docetic/spiritualizing error (protestant_trap). B is correct and the hardest nuance: temporal death and the FIRST spiritual death (from the Fall) are overcome unconditionally so all are resurrected and brought back to be judged, but a SECOND spiritual death — final separation — is suffered conditionally by those who do not repent. Tests the precise conditional/unconditional asymmetry of the two-deaths framework, not generic 'Jesus saves everyone.'
