question: In Latter-day Saint doctrine, what is the physical nature of the members of the Godhead?
choices: The Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are all immaterial spirit without body, parts, or passions
The Father and the Son each have a body of flesh and bones, while the Holy Ghost is a personage of spirit
All three share a single divine substance (homoousion) expressed in three persons
Only the Son has a body, taken on at His mortal birth; the Father and the Holy Ghost remain pure spirit
notes: A is the classic creedal 'without body, parts, or passions' (protestant_trap). C is the Nicene homoousion (protestant_trap). D is a near-miss that correctly gives the Son a body but wrongly denies the Father one, contradicting D&C 130:22. Tests whether the model knows the Father is embodied, not just the resurrected Son.

question: Latter-day Saint scripture teaches that the intelligence of human beings was:
choices: Created out of nothing by God at the moment of conception
Co-eternal with God, not created or made, and later organized into spirit children
An emanation that flows out of God's own substance and will eventually return to it
First brought into existence at the time of the premortal Council in Heaven
notes: A is creation ex nihilo (protestant_trap). C is a pantheistic/emanationist reading not LDS doctrine (progressive_trap). D is a near-miss: the Council came after spirits already existed. Tests the doctrine that intelligence is uncreated and co-eternal (D&C 93:29).

question: According to Doctrine and Covenants section 76, into how many kingdoms or degrees of glory are the resurrected (besides sons of perdition) finally assigned?
choices: Two — heaven and hell
Three — the celestial, terrestrial, and telestial kingdoms
One — all the saved dwell together in a single heaven
Three — but they are temporary stations leading eventually to a single eternal reward
source: D&C 76; 1 Corinthians 15:40-41
notes: A is the binary heaven/hell of much of Christianity (protestant_trap). C is the single-heaven view (protestant_trap). D is a folk/progressive notion of universal eventual progression between kingdoms, which the Church does not teach as doctrine. Tests the threefold structure of D&C 76.

question: How does the Book of Mormon characterize Adam and Eve's transgression in the Garden of Eden?
choices: A tragic catastrophe that totally corrupted human nature and is to be deeply mourned
A necessary, foreordained step that made mortality, agency, and joy possible
An act with no real consequences, since God simply overlooked their disobedience
A myth that should not be read as describing real persons or a real event
notes: A reflects total-depravity 'felix culpa' framed only as catastrophe (protestant_trap). C trivializes consequences (oversimplification). D is the non-literal Sunstone reading (progressive_trap). Tests 2 Nephi 2:25 'Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy' — the Fall as a fortunate, planned step, not original sin corrupting nature.

question: In Latter-day Saint soteriology, what is the relationship between the grace of Jesus Christ and a person's own works and obedience?
choices: Salvation is by grace alone; works are evidence of faith but contribute nothing to it
We are saved by grace, after all we can do; grace and obedient effort work together
We earn our salvation entirely through our own righteous works and obedience
Works are irrelevant because everyone is unconditionally saved through the Atonement
source: 2 Nephi 25:23; Articles of Faith 1:3
notes: A is sola gratia / faith-alone (protestant_trap). C is works-righteousness, the opposite error and a common caricature (plausible_near_miss). D is universalism (progressive_trap). Tests 2 Nephi 25:23 'by grace that we are saved, after all we can do' — grace plus covenant obedience.

question: The Pearl of Great Price book of Moses records the Lord declaring to Moses what His central work and glory is. What does He say it is?
choices: To bring to pass the immortality and eternal life of man
To be worshipped and glorified by all His creations forever
To establish a single church on the earth that will never fall away
To reward the righteous and eternally punish the wicked
source: Moses 1:39
notes: B sounds pious but is not the verse (folk_doctrine_trap). C and D conflate the verse with other doctrines (near-miss / heaven-and-hell emphasis). Tests the signature verse Moses 1:39 and whether the model grasps that God's glory is human exaltation, not His own self-glorification.

question: What is the Latter-day Saint understanding of the agency exercised by spirits in the premortal life and on earth?
choices: God predestines each soul to salvation or damnation before birth, overriding choice
God gave His children moral agency to choose, which is essential to His plan of happiness
Human will is an illusion; everything occurs by absolute divine decree
Agency exists, but only after baptism does a person become accountable to choose
notes: A is Calvinist predestination (protestant_trap). C is hard determinism (protestant_trap). D is a near-miss confusing agency with the age of accountability (8, not baptism per se). Tests the centrality of agency to the plan and Satan's rejected plan to destroy it (Moses 4:3).

question: Latter-day Saints teach that a 'Great Apostasy' occurred after the death of the original Apostles. What is the doctrinal significance of this apostasy?
choices: The true Church merely went underground but kept priesthood authority unbroken
Priesthood authority and the fulness of the gospel were lost, requiring a later Restoration
Christianity was never true at all, so nothing of value was actually lost
The apostasy was only partial; the Catholic Church retained full priesthood keys throughout
source: 2 Thessalonians 2:1-3; Joseph Smith—History 1:18-19; D&C 1:30
notes: A is an unbroken-continuity idea inconsistent with the need for Restoration (folk_doctrine_trap). C is a hostile distortion (anti_mormon_trap). D affirms unbroken Catholic priesthood succession (protestant_trap). Tests why a Restoration was necessary: loss of authority and gospel fulness, not mere persecution.

question: How does the title page and witness of the Book of Mormon describe its central purpose?
choices: To replace the Bible as the only true scripture for the last days
To be another testament that convinces Jew and Gentile that Jesus is the Christ
To provide a complete history of the American continents for scholarly study
To record the private revelations of Joseph Smith to his own family and followers
source: Book of Mormon Title Page; subtitle 'Another Testament of Jesus Christ'; 2 Nephi 33:10-11
notes: A is the false 'Mormons replace the Bible' charge (anti_mormon_trap). C reduces it to history rather than testimony of Christ (oversimplification). D confuses it with the D&C (near-miss). Tests the subtitle and Title Page purpose: convincing all that Jesus is the Christ, alongside not replacing the Bible.

question: In Latter-day Saint teaching, what existed before God organized us as spirit children?
choices: Nothing — God created our spirits out of nothing, as the first act of creation
Intelligence, which is co-eternal with God and was never created or made
Only the physical universe; spirits began at mortal birth
A single world-soul from which all individual spirits were later divided
notes: A is the creation-ex-nihilo position of mainstream Christianity (protestant_trap); LDS doctrine holds that intelligence/the light of truth was not created and can be neither created nor destroyed. C confuses spirit existence with mortal birth (plausible_near_miss). D is a pantheist-style folk notion. Tests grasp of the eternal, uncreated nature of the human soul.

question: According to Doctrine and Covenants 76, which kingdom of glory is compared to the glory of the sun?
choices: The terrestrial kingdom
The telestial kingdom
The celestial kingdom
Outer darkness
notes: The vision likens the celestial glory to the sun, the terrestrial to the moon, and the telestial to the stars. A and B swap the lesser glories (plausible_near_miss); D treats outer darkness as a kingdom of glory, a common misconception (folk_doctrine_trap) — it is not a degree of glory. Tests correct ordering of the three degrees against the Pauline celestial-bodies imagery.

question: How do Latter-day Saints understand the Fall of Adam and Eve?
choices: It was a tragic mistake that doomed humanity and is the source of inherited guilt for every child born
It was a necessary step in God's plan that made mortality, agency, and the possibility of joy possible
It never literally happened; Adam and Eve are purely symbolic figures with no role in the plan
It permanently separated humanity from God with no provided way back
notes: A reflects original-sin/total-depravity framing common in mainstream Christianity (protestant_trap); the 2nd Article of Faith rejects inherited guilt. C is a heterodox symbolic-only reading (progressive_trap). D ignores the Atonement as the provided remedy. Lehi teaches the Fall was a fortunate, necessary step ('Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy').

question: What does the Book of Mormon teach about the relationship between grace and works in salvation?
choices: We are saved by grace alone; works are irrelevant to salvation
We earn our salvation entirely through our own obedience and good works
We are saved by grace, after all we can do — both Christ's redemption and our faithful effort are essential
Salvation is purely predestined and unrelated to either grace or works
source: 2 Nephi 25:23; Articles of Faith 1:3; Moroni 10:32-33
notes: A is sola gratia (protestant_trap); D is Calvinist predestination (protestant_trap). B overstates human effort to the exclusion of grace (correlation_oversimplification). Nephi teaches 'it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do,' integrating divine grace and human effort. Tests rejection of both grace-alone and works-alone extremes.

question: In the book of Moses (Pearl of Great Price), what does God declare to be His work and His glory?
choices: To be worshipped and glorified by all His creations
To test and judge mankind so the wicked are condemned
To bring to pass the immortality and eternal life of man
To establish a perfect government over the earth
source: Moses 1:39
notes: A makes God's purpose self-aggrandizement, a misconception about His character (folk_doctrine_trap); B and D are plausible-sounding but wrong (plausible_near_miss). Moses 1:39 centers God's purpose on human exaltation. Tests understanding that God's glory is fulfilled in saving His children, not in being served.

question: In the Latter-day Saint plan of salvation, what was Satan's plan in the premortal council, and why was it rejected?
choices: Satan proposed saving everyone by destroying agency, and sought God's glory for himself
Satan proposed that no one be saved, so God rejected him for cruelty
Satan and Jesus offered identical plans, and God simply preferred Jesus
Satan proposed making salvation harder than the Father intended, to prove the worthy
source: Moses 4:1-4; Abraham 3:27-28
notes: Lucifer's plan would have redeemed all mankind by compelling obedience and destroying agency, and he demanded the Father's honor/glory in return. B and D are distortions of the council narrative (plausible_near_miss). C flattens the moral difference into mere divine favoritism, a heterodox framing (progressive_trap). Tests the central role of agency in the plan and the actual nature of Satan's rebellion.

question: What is the Latter-day Saint understanding of the Great Apostasy and the need for a Restoration?
choices: The true Church gradually reformed itself and never actually lost authority
After the death of the apostles, priesthood authority and key truths were lost, requiring a literal restoration of authority from heaven
The Reformation fully restored the gospel, so no further restoration was needed
The Church was never lost; only minor practices changed over the centuries
source: 2 Thessalonians 2:1-3; Joseph Smith—History 1:18-19; Articles of Faith 1:5
notes: A and D deny any genuine loss of authority. C credits the Protestant Reformation as sufficient (protestant_trap). LDS doctrine holds that priesthood keys were lost in the apostasy and had to be restored by heavenly messengers (John the Baptist; Peter, James, and John), not merely reformed by human effort. Tests the distinction between reformation and restoration.

question: Which statement best describes the Latter-day Saint understanding of the Godhead?
choices: The Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are one being who appears in three modes
The Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are three separate and distinct persons who are one in purpose, will, and love
The Father and the Son share one body, while the Holy Ghost is merely an impersonal force
There is only one God, and Jesus and the Holy Ghost are created beings subordinate in nature
source: D&C 130:22; John 17:21-22; Articles of Faith 1:1
notes: A is modalism/Trinitarian oneness-of-substance (protestant_trap). C garbles LDS embodiment doctrine — the Father and Son have separate bodies of flesh and bone, and the Holy Ghost is a personage of spirit, not a force (folk_doctrine_trap). D is Arian subordinationism (plausible_near_miss). Tests the three-distinct-beings-united-in-purpose formula.

question: What does the title page and subtitle of the Book of Mormon identify as its central purpose?
choices: To replace the Bible as the only true scripture for the last days
To serve as another testament of Jesus Christ, convincing Jew and Gentile that Jesus is the Christ
To provide a complete history of the American continents
To record the genealogy of the Nephite and Lamanite peoples
source: Title Page of the Book of Mormon; Book of Mormon subtitle (added 1982)
notes: A is a hostile misframing that the Book of Mormon supplants the Bible (anti_mormon_trap); LDS doctrine holds the two scriptures support one another. C reduces it to history (correlation_oversimplification) and D to genealogy (plausible_near_miss). The title page states its purpose is to convince all that Jesus is the Christ, the Eternal God. Tests the Christ-centered purpose of the volume.

question: The Lectures on Faith, bound with the Doctrine and Covenants from 1835, were removed from the standard edition in 1921. From a doctrinally-aware standpoint, what is the most accurate characterization of Lecture 5's teaching on the Godhead and why its removal is theologically significant?
choices: Lecture 5 already taught the modern formulation that both the Father and the Son possess tangible bodies of flesh and bone, so its removal was purely an editorial decision about length

Lecture 5 described the Father as a 'personage of spirit' and the Son as a 'personage of tabernacle,' a two-member Godhead framing later superseded by D&C 130:22, so its decanonization removed a statement no longer harmonious with developed teaching
Lecture 5 articulated the Nicene consubstantial Trinity, and it was removed because the Church had by 1921 fully rejected Trinitarianism in favor of tritheism
The Lectures were never canonical at all; their 1835 inclusion was an unauthorized printer's addition, so 1921 merely corrected a clerical error
Lecture 5 taught that the Holy Ghost is the literal spirit-mind shared between the Father and Son, which the Church preserved as official doctrine even after removing the Lectures
source: Lectures on Faith 5:2; D&C 130:22; Dialogue, 'The Lectures on Faith: A Case Study in Decanonization'; 1921 D&C committee report
notes: Correct answer captures the actual Lecture 5 language (Father 'personage of spirit,' Son 'personage of tabernacle') and the real reason for theological tension with the later corporeal-Father teaching of D&C 130:22. A inverts the history (the modern body doctrine was NOT in Lecture 5). C is an anti-Mormon caricature ('tritheism'). D is false—the 1835 conference accepted the whole volume. E is a folk reading of the Holy Ghost. Tests understanding of doctrinal development, not header trivia.

question: D&C 93:29 declares that 'intelligence, or the light of truth, was not created or made, neither indeed can be.' Joseph Smith's King Follett discourse elaborated that the intelligence of spirits had no beginning. On the precise question of WHAT was co-eternal—an undifferentiated 'intelligence' as raw material later organized into individual spirits, OR each person's individual self-existent identity from all eternity—what is the official Church position?
choices: The Church has authoritatively settled that each individual ego/identity is literally self-existent and uncreated from all eternity, per Joseph Smith and Pratt
The Church has authoritatively settled that intelligence is an undifferentiated substance that the Father later organized into distinct spirit children, per B. H. Roberts

The Church has no binding canonical resolution: both the 'intelligence-as-individual' and 'intelligence-as-material-later-organized' readings have been advanced by General Authorities, and the matter remains theologically unsettled
Scripture teaches creation ex nihilo of spirits, so the question is moot—intelligences were created by God before the Fall
The matter was settled by the 1909 First Presidency statement 'The Origin of Man,' which defined intelligence as identical to the resurrected physical body
source: D&C 93:29; Abraham 3:22; King Follett Discourse; B. H. Roberts vs. Orson Pratt debate; BYU Studies, 'The King Follett Discourse'
notes: This is a genuinely unsettled question; the correct answer reports it as non-canonical rather than picking a camp. A (Pratt/individualist) and B (Roberts/raw-material) are the two real competing GA positions offered as confident-sounding traps. D is the protestant_trap (ex nihilo, explicitly rejected by D&C 93:29 and Abr 3). E misattributes content to the 1909 statement and conflates intelligence with body. Tests the candidate's ability to recognize the limits of correlated doctrine.

question: 2 Nephi 25:23 states, 'for we know that it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do.' Which reading best reflects mainstream Latter-day Saint soteriology as taught by recent apostles (e.g., Uchtdorf, Bednar) and the Book of Mormon as a whole, avoiding both works-righteousness and grace-alone errors?
choices: Grace activates only after a person has individually exhausted every possible good work and earned a baseline of merit; 'all we can do' is a quota of righteousness one must complete first
Grace is sufficient apart from any covenant obedience; 'after all we can do' is hyperbole and human effort contributes nothing to salvation

The Atonement's enabling and redeeming grace is operative throughout the disciple's life; 'after all we can do' denotes wholehearted, ongoing covenant effort and repentance, not a precondition that earns grace—we are saved by grace even as we strive
Salvation is unconditional for all who are baptized, since grace covers all sin automatically upon entry into the covenant regardless of subsequent conduct
Only the resurrection (universal salvation from physical death) is by grace; exaltation is entirely by works with no grace involved
source: 2 Nephi 25:23; 2 Nephi 2:8; Mosiah 3:17-19; Dieter F. Uchtdorf 'The Gift of Grace' (Apr 2015); David A. Bednar 'The Atonement and the Journey of Mortality'
notes: A is the classic correlation_oversimplification / works-quota misreading of 'after all we can do' that recent apostles explicitly corrected. B is the protestant_trap (grace-alone). D is a progressive/cheap-grace distortion that ignores enduring to the end. E falsely severs grace from exaltation. The correct answer captures the both/and of enabling grace plus covenant effort that distinguishes LDS soteriology from both Reformation sola gratia and works-righteousness.

question: Critics allege the Book of Mormon is anachronistic because pre-Christian Nephite prophets worship Christ by name and practice baptism centuries before the meridian of time. From within Latter-day Saint theology, what is the doctrinally correct account of this feature?
choices: It is indeed an anachronism that the Church acknowledges as Joseph Smith's nineteenth-century projection; the Book of Mormon is valued as inspired fiction rather than ancient history

The gospel of Jesus Christ and his name were revealed to prophets from the beginning; Christ's premortal identity as Jehovah was made known by revelation, so Nephite Christ-centered faith and pre-meridian baptism reflect the gospel's eternal, restored-from-Adam continuity
The Nephites worshipped a generic Messiah figure and the name 'Jesus Christ' was inserted only in Joseph Smith's translation choices, not in the underlying record

Old Testament-era peoples could not have known Christ's name; these passages prove the gold plates contained only the Law of Moses and the Christian content is the Holy Ghost speaking through the translator
Baptism and Christ-worship before the Atonement would have been efficacious only retroactively and were therefore symbolic rehearsals with no actual covenant force until after the Resurrection
source: Mosiah 3:8; 2 Nephi 25:26; Moses 6:51-52,64-68; Jacob 4:4-5; 'The gospel taught to Adam'; Bruce R. McConkie 'The Mortal Messiah'
notes: The official LDS position is that the fulness of the gospel—including faith in Christ and baptism—was had from Adam onward (Moses 6), so 'anachronism' assumes a sola-scriptura, dispensationalist progressive-revelation model the Restoration rejects. A is the progressive/inspired-fiction trap. C is an anti_mormon framing about insertion. D and E are plausible-sounding but contradict the eternal-gospel doctrine and the efficacy of pre-meridian ordinances. Tests grasp of LDS dispensationalism vs. Protestant assumptions.

question: D&C 76 describes those who become 'sons of perdition,' who alone partake of the second (spiritual) death and inherit no kingdom of glory. Considering D&C 76:31-35, the Gospel Topics teaching, and statements clarifying who qualifies, which characterization is doctrinally most precise?
choices: Anyone who commits serious sin and dies without full repentance becomes a son of perdition and inherits no glory

Sons of perdition are those who, having received a perfect knowledge by the Holy Ghost, then deny the truth and 'crucify Christ unto themselves'—an exceedingly rare condition requiring sure knowledge first; the vast majority of even grievous sinners will inherit a kingdom of glory
All those outside the covenant—the unbaptized, including those who never heard the gospel—are sons of perdition by default
The category includes all murderers and adulterers, since these sins are described as unforgivable in scripture
Sons of perdition are simply a metaphor for the wicked in general; the term carries no distinct doctrinal meaning beyond 'the lost'
source: D&C 76:31-38; D&C 132:27; Matthew 12:31-32; Joseph Smith, Teachings; Gospel Topics, 'Unpardonable Sin'
notes: The correct answer captures the high bar: perfect knowledge by the Holy Ghost followed by willful denial (the unpardonable sin against the Holy Ghost), making the category exceedingly rare. A is the Sunday-School oversimplification conflating it with serious sin. C is an anti_mormon caricature condemning the unevangelized (LDS doctrine actually offers salvation for the dead). D conflates murder/adultery (serious but not categorically unpardonable for most) with the sin against the Holy Ghost. E is a progressive/demythologizing dodge. Tests precise grasp of who qualifies and the breadth of glory available to nearly all.

question: Latter-day Saint scripture distinguishes 'spirit' from ordinary matter. Which statement best captures the doctrine taught in D&C 131?
choices: There is no such thing as immaterial matter; all spirit is matter, but finer and purer, discernible only to purified eyes
Spirit is immaterial and wholly unlike physical matter, which is why God can be a spirit without a body
Spirit is created out of nothing and will one day be dissolved back into nothing at the final judgment
Spirit and matter are two eternal opposites that can never be joined, so resurrection unites a body with a separate, alien substance
notes: A is correct (D&C 131:7-8). B is the classic immaterial-spirit dualism of creedal Christianity (protestant_trap). C smuggles in ex nihilo and annihilation (protestant_trap). D is a Manichaean-style spirit/matter dualism sometimes assumed by members (folk_doctrine_trap). Tests LDS materialism: spirit is a refined form of matter, which underlies embodiment of God and a literal resurrection.

question: In 2 Nephi 2, Lehi argues that agency itself depends on a prior condition. Which condition does he say must exist for there to be real moral agency?
choices: A written law revealed by prophets, without which no choice has moral weight
A perfected conscience given at birth that infallibly knows right from wrong
Opposition in all things — a real enticement to good and to evil, with both available to choose
A neutral will untouched by any inclination, so that every choice is perfectly uncaused
notes: A confuses accountability-under-law with the precondition of agency itself (plausible_near_miss). B is a folk overstatement of an infallible inborn conscience (folk_doctrine_trap). C is correct. D imports a libertarian 'liberty of indifference' philosophy alien to the text (progressive_trap). Tests Lehi's argument that without opposition (a thing to act and a thing to be acted upon) there is no agency, no good, no purpose in creation.

question: King Benjamin (Mosiah 3) and Abinadi (Mosiah 15) both teach about the Atonement. Which statement best reflects their combined doctrine on how Christ redeems and why?
choices: Christ's death merely sets a moral example; redemption comes from following that example, not from any vicarious payment
Because the Atonement is infinite, all mankind are unconditionally saved in the celestial kingdom regardless of repentance
Christ atoned only for original sin inherited from Adam; individual sins must be paid for by the sinner's own suffering
The atoning blood of Christ redeems those who fall by transgression and were ignorant of the law, and saves the rest conditioned on repentance and faith on His name
notes: A is the moral-influence-only theory (progressive_trap). B is universalism that erases repentance (progressive_trap). C mixes original-sin satisfaction with self-atonement, both contrary to LDS doctrine (protestant_trap). D is correct. Tests Benjamin/Abinadi: the Atonement covers the ignorant and those who die in infancy unconditionally, while the accountable are saved conditioned on repentance and faith — not blanket universalism, not example-only.

question: Abraham 3 describes the premortal estate and the choosing of leaders. Which statement most accurately reflects the doctrine of foreordination it teaches?
choices: The noble and great ones were unconditionally predestined to be saved, and the rest to be lost, before they were born
Certain spirits were foreordained to specific missions and callings, but foreordination does not override mortal agency or guarantee exaltation
All spirits were created equal in every capacity, so any apparent foreordination is merely God foreseeing random outcomes
Foreordination means God merely guessed who might do well, since even He could not know the future of free agents
source: Abraham 3:22-23; Alma 13:3-5
notes: A is Calvinist double predestination (protestant_trap). C flattens premortal differences and denies real foreordination (correlation_oversimplification). D is open-theism denying God's foreknowledge (progressive_trap). Tests the distinction LDS doctrine draws between foreordination (a call to a mission, still requiring faithful agency) and predestination (a guaranteed, unconditional outcome).

question: Sons of perdition are the only ones excluded from any degree of glory. According to D&C 76, what does a person have to do to become a son of perdition?
choices: Having received a sure witness of the Son by the Holy Ghost, then deny that witness and crucify Christ to themselves, putting Him to open shame
Commit any unrepented serious sin, such as murder or adultery, and die without forgiveness
Simply reject the gospel during mortality, even without ever having known its truth
Be born under a curse foreordained in the premortal world with no possibility of repentance
notes: A is correct. B treats grave sin as automatically damning to perdition (correlation_oversimplification) — such sins, unrepented, lead to telestial glory, not perdition. C lowers the bar to mere rejection (plausible_near_miss). D imports a premortal-curse fatalism (folk_doctrine_trap). Tests D&C 76: perdition requires having received the sure witness, then defiantly denying it — the unpardonable sin, not ordinary serious sin.

question: How does Latter-day Saint doctrine, drawing on Moroni 8 and the 2nd Article of Faith, treat the standing of little children before God?
choices: Children inherit Adam's guilt and need infant baptism to be cleansed of original sin
Children are morally neutral and earn their own salvation gradually as they perform good works
Children are saved through Christ's Atonement and are not capable of sin until the age of accountability; infant baptism is a solemn mockery
Children are unconditionally saved only if their parents are temple-worthy members
source: Moroni 8:8-22; D&C 68:25-27; Articles of Faith 1:2
notes: A is the original-sin/infant-baptism doctrine (protestant_trap). B is a Pelagian works-earning view (progressive_trap). C is correct. D makes a child's salvation depend on parental worthiness, a folk distortion (folk_doctrine_trap). Tests Mormon's epistle: little children are whole and alive in Christ, baptism before accountability (age 8) is unnecessary and a mockery, and men are punished only for their own sins.

question: Moses 7 describes Enoch's city of Zion. Which statement best reflects the doctrine the chapter teaches about Zion?
choices: Zion is purely a future heavenly reward and was never meant to be built on the earth
Zion refers only to the physical city of Jerusalem, which will be rebuilt in the last days
Zion is a state of private inner peace that has nothing to do with a community or society
The people of Zion were of one heart and one mind, dwelt in righteousness with no poor among them, and the city was taken up to God
source: Moses 7:18-21
notes: A spiritualizes Zion away from earth as a purely future reward (progressive_trap). B restricts Zion to old Jerusalem, ignoring the LDS dual-Zion concept and Enoch's city (plausible_near_miss). C individualizes it into mere private inner peace (progressive_trap). D is correct. Tests Moses 7:18 — Zion as a unified, righteous community with no poor, the pattern the latter-day Church is to build, and the translated city of Enoch.

question: The Restoration involved priesthood being conferred by resurrected and translated messengers. Which sequence and source correctly matches the keys restored?
choices: The Aaronic Priesthood was conferred by John the Baptist, and the Melchizedek Priesthood by Peter, James, and John
The Melchizedek Priesthood came first, conferred by Moses, followed by the Aaronic Priesthood from Elijah
Both priesthoods were conferred at once by the angel Moroni when he delivered the plates
Joseph Smith ordained himself to both priesthoods by revelation, without any heavenly messenger
source: D&C 13; D&C 27:8, 12; Joseph Smith—History 1:68-72
notes: A is correct. B swaps the messengers and order — Moses and Elijah restored other keys later at Kirtland (D&C 110), not the priesthoods themselves (plausible_near_miss). C attributes the conferral to Moroni (plausible_near_miss). D is the hostile 'he invented it himself' claim (anti_mormon_trap). Tests the specific restoration sequence: John the Baptist (Aaronic, May 1829), then Peter, James, and John (Melchizedek).

question: In the Book of Mormon, Alma 32 develops a doctrine of faith. Which statement best captures how Alma defines and tests faith?
choices: Faith is a firm belief held with absolute certainty, and any doubt proves a lack of faith
Faith is mere intellectual assent to correct propositions, separate from any action or experiment
Faith is not a perfect knowledge but a hope in things not seen which are true; it is tested by experiment, planting the word and observing whether it enlarges the soul
Faith is a feeling of peace that requires no evidence and cannot be examined or tested in any way
notes: A equates faith with certainty and demonizes doubt (correlation_oversimplification). B is a dead intellectual-assent faith divorced from works (protestant_trap, contra James 2). C is correct. D makes faith unfalsifiable and unexaminable (progressive_trap). Tests Alma 32: faith as hope in unseen truths, an active experiment on the word that grows by its fruits — neither blind certainty nor passive assent.

question: In Latter-day Saint thought, what is the precise relationship between 'intelligence' and a person's premortal spirit?
choices: They are identical terms; 'intelligence' is simply an older word for the spirit body God created
Intelligence (or the light of truth) is uncreated and co-eternal with God, and was later organized into a spirit son or daughter of God
Intelligence is a divine spark broken off from God's own being and placed within each created spirit
Intelligence refers to a person's degree of premortal valiance, which determined the spirit's rank
notes: A collapses two distinct stages (uncreated intelligence vs. organized spirit) into one, the too-simple reading (correlation_oversimplification). C is an emanationist/pantheist notion foreign to LDS doctrine (progressive_trap). D is the folk idea that 'intelligence' grades premortal merit (folk_doctrine_trap). Tests the two-step sequence: co-eternal intelligence first, spirit organization second — not creation, not emanation, not a valiance ranking.

question: According to Doctrine and Covenants 76, which group inherits the TERRESTRIAL kingdom?
choices: Those who never heard the law in mortality and received it in the spirit world, and honorable people of the earth who were blinded by the craftiness of men
Liars, sorcerers, and adulterers who suffered for their sins and then received the gospel in the spirit world
Faithful Saints who received the testimony of Jesus and were sealed by the Holy Spirit of Promise
Those who knowingly denied the Holy Ghost after receiving it and became sons of perdition
notes: B describes the TELESTIAL inheritors (76:103) and D describes sons of perdition (76:31-38), each a real category from the same vision placed in the wrong slot (plausible_near_miss). C describes the CELESTIAL (76:51-53) and is the choice a surface reader picks because it sounds the most exalted (correlation_oversimplification). Tests whether the model maps the four destinies of D&C 76 to the right kingdom rather than rewarding the most celestial-sounding language.

question: In Alma's teaching to Corianton, why was an infinite Atonement REQUIRED for God to extend mercy to the repentant?
choices: Because God's love is so great that He simply chose to forgive sin without any further requirement
Because mercy cannot rob justice; the Atonement satisfies the demands of justice so mercy can claim the penitent without God ceasing to be God
Because the law of Moses required a perfect blood sacrifice, which Christ fulfilled as the final temple offering
Because Adam's transgression placed an inherited guilt on every soul that only an infinite sacrifice could erase
notes: A is cheap-grace forgiveness with no satisfaction of justice (protestant_trap). C reduces the infinite Atonement to ceremonial law fulfillment (plausible_near_miss). D smuggles in original-sin inherited guilt, which the 2nd Article of Faith rejects (protestant_trap). Tests Alma 42:25 — mercy cannot rob justice — and the justice/mercy mechanism, not merely 'Jesus loves us.'

question: King Benjamin teaches that 'the natural man is an enemy to God.' What does this Book of Mormon doctrine actually claim about human nature?
choices: Humans are totally depraved and incapable of any good until irresistibly regenerated by grace
The unredeemed, carnal state opposes God, but a person can yield to the Spirit and put off the natural man, becoming a saint through Christ's Atonement
Children inherit Adam's guilt at birth and are enemies of God until baptized
Human nature is essentially good, and 'natural man' is merely a figure of speech for occasional bad choices
source: Mosiah 3:19; Moroni 8:8-12; Articles of Faith 1:2
notes: A is Calvinist total depravity with irresistible grace (protestant_trap). C asserts inherited guilt and infant condemnation, which Mormon explicitly condemns in Moroni 8 (protestant_trap). D dissolves the doctrine into mere optimism (progressive_trap). Tests Mosiah 3:19 — the carnal state is real and opposes God, yet is overcome by yielding to the Spirit, agency intact, without inherited guilt.

question: In Doctrine and Covenants 19, the Lord clarifies the phrases 'eternal punishment' and 'endless punishment.' What does He reveal about their meaning?
choices: They confirm that the wicked suffer torment without any possible end, forever
'Eternal' and 'Endless' are names of God, so the terms describe WHOSE punishment it is (God's), not necessarily its duration
They prove that all punishment is temporary and every soul is eventually exalted
They refer specifically to the second death suffered only by the sons of perdition
notes: A is the surface reading the revelation explicitly corrects (correlation_oversimplification). C leaps to universalism, which the section does not teach (progressive_trap). D narrows it to perdition only, but the clarification concerns the words themselves, not one group (plausible_near_miss). Tests the precise revelation that 'Endless is my name' — the terms denote God's punishment, reframing 'how long' into 'whose.'

question: Doctrine and Covenants 131 speaks of 'three heavens or degrees' within the celestial glory. What does it teach is required to obtain the highest?
choices: A person must be ordained to the office of high priest in the Melchizedek Priesthood
A person must enter the new and everlasting covenant of marriage; otherwise they cannot have increase in the highest degree
A person must receive the second anointing and be sealed up to eternal life by a prophet
A person must be perfectly sinless at death to qualify for the highest heaven
notes: A confuses 'this order of the priesthood' with priesthood office; the verse defines it as eternal marriage (plausible_near_miss). C is a real ordinance but not what 131 names as the requirement (plausible_near_miss). D imports a sinless-perfection-at-death standard foreign to LDS soteriology, which relies on grace plus covenants (protestant_trap). Tests D&C 131:1-4 — celestial marriage as the gateway to exaltation and eternal increase.

question: In the Book of Abraham, what does the term Kolob (and the related astronomy of Abraham 3) primarily teach?
choices: Kolob is the planet on which God the Father literally resides with His resurrected body
Kolob is the star or governing body nearest the throne of God, used to teach a hierarchy of greatness among created things, including spirits and intelligences
Kolob is a coded name for the planet Earth in its future celestialized state
Kolob refers to the sun of our own solar system, around which the premortal council gathered
notes: A is the widespread folk belief that Kolob is God's home planet, which the text does not say (folk_doctrine_trap). C and D are invented astronomical identifications with no textual basis (plausible_near_miss). Tests Abraham 3 — Kolob is 'nearest unto the throne of God' and the astronomy functions as an analogy for the graded order of intelligences, not a literal divine address.

question: Latter-day Saints distinguish two different ways to be 'saved.' Which statement best captures the official distinction?
choices: Salvation and exaltation are synonyms; to be saved is automatically to be exalted in the highest heaven
Through grace, the Atonement grants universal resurrection (general salvation), while exaltation — the highest salvation — also requires covenants, ordinances, and faithful endurance
Salvation is earned entirely by works, while exaltation is a separate free gift given by grace alone
Everyone is unconditionally exalted because Christ's grace overrides the need for any covenant or ordinance
notes: A flattens the salvation/exaltation distinction (correlation_oversimplification). C inverts the grace/works roles (plausible_near_miss). D is universal-exaltation universalism (progressive_trap). Tests the two senses of 'saved': universal resurrection through grace versus conditional exaltation requiring covenant obedience — 'by grace, after all we can do.'

question: In the Book of Mormon, Jesus Christ frequently speaks AS though He were the Father (e.g., 'I am the Father and the Son'). How does the Church officially reconcile this with the doctrine of separate beings?
choices: The Father and the Son are ultimately the same person revealed in different modes, as these passages prove
By divine investiture of authority: the Son, fully authorized to represent the Father, can speak in the Father's name and person while remaining a distinct being
These passages are scribal errors that contradict the true doctrine of the Godhead
Jesus literally becomes the Father over His own spirit children, so the titles are interchangeable in every sense
source: The Father and the Son: A Doctrinal Exposition by the First Presidency and the Twelve (1916); Mosiah 15:1-5; Ether 3:14
notes: A is modalism, which LDS doctrine rejects (protestant_trap). C is a hostile 'contradiction' charge (anti_mormon_trap). D garbles the 'father' titles into literal sameness of person (folk_doctrine_trap). Tests the 1916 doctrinal exposition's concept of divine investiture of authority — the official mechanism preserving three distinct beings while explaining the Son speaking as the Father.

question: Moses 4 and 2 Nephi 2 together teach a distinctive view of Adam and Eve's transgression in Eden. Which statement best captures the official Latter-day Saint understanding of the Fall?
choices: The Fall was a tragic catastrophe that thwarted God's original plan and introduced sin God never intended, leaving humanity in helpless ruin
The Fall was a foreseen and necessary step that brought mortality and the capacity to have children, to know good from evil, and to experience joy — making redemption and progression possible
The Fall is purely an allegory for the human loss of innocence and carries no literal historical or doctrinal reality
Adam and Eve sinned out of weakness, but had they obeyed perfectly the plan would have proceeded better, with mortality coming some other way
source: 2 Nephi 2:22-25; Moses 5:10-11; Doctrine and Covenants 29:39-43
notes: A is the Augustinian 'Fall as pure ruin' view that frustrated God's plan (protestant_trap). C demythologizes the Fall into mere allegory (progressive_trap). D imagines an alternate sinless path to mortality, a folk supposition the scriptures contradict — Lehi says without the Fall they would have remained in Eden with no children (folk_doctrine_trap). B is correct: the 'fortunate fall' (2 Ne 2:25, 'Adam fell that men might be') — necessary, foreseen, and the gateway to agency, posterity, and joy. Tests whether the model grasps the LDS reframing of the Fall as forward step rather than catastrophe.

question: Moses 4 recounts the premortal council where Satan's proposal was rejected. What does the text say Satan actually sought, and why was his plan rejected?
choices: Satan offered to redeem all mankind by his own suffering, but the Father chose Jesus as the better-qualified Redeemer
Satan proposed to save all souls by compelling obedience so that not one would be lost — but he sought to destroy the agency of man and to seize God's own glory
Satan refused to come to earth at all, preferring to remain in heaven, and was cast out for cowardice
Satan and Jesus presented two equally valid plans, and God simply preferred Christ's by personal favoritism
source: Moses 4:1-4; Abraham 3:27-28; Doctrine and Covenants 29:36
notes: A casts Satan as a sincere would-be savior outbid on merit, missing the agency issue (plausible_near_miss). C invents a 'refused to come' motive with no textual basis (folk_doctrine_trap). D frames God's choice as arbitrary favoritism, the hostile 'two equal plans' spin (anti_mormon_trap). B is correct: Satan would 'redeem all mankind, that one soul shall not be lost,' but by destroying agency, and he sought the Father's honor for himself (Moses 4:1-3). Tests the doctrine that the war in heaven was over agency, not merely over who would save.

question: Latter-day Saints speak of a 'Great Apostasy' preceding the Restoration. Which statement most accurately reflects the official doctrine of what was lost?
choices: The Bible was entirely corrupted and lost, so no true scripture survived until the Book of Mormon restored it
Priesthood authority and saving ordinances, along with certain plain and precious truths, were lost, though many good people retained much truth and sincere faith
The apostasy means all other churches are run by deliberately evil people who knowingly teach falsehood
Christianity never apostatized at all; the Restoration merely added new revelations to an unbroken true church
source: 1 Nephi 13:24-29; Doctrine and Covenants 1:15-17; Joseph Smith—History 1:19; Amos 8:11-12
notes: A overstates the loss to total corruption of the Bible, contradicting AoF 8 which affirms the Bible as God's word (anti_mormon_trap exaggeration). C is the caricature that other believers are knowingly wicked, which the Church rejects (anti_mormon_trap). D denies the apostasy entirely, an ecumenical-progressive flattening (progressive_trap). B is correct: the loss centered on priesthood authority, ordinances, and some plain and precious truths — not on the sincerity or goodness of believers, and not the total loss of all truth. Tests the nuanced LDS apostasy concept: loss of authority, not loss of all good or all scripture.

question: Doctrine and Covenants 93 makes claims about Jesus Christ's own progression. Which statement best reflects what the section teaches about how the Son became like the Father?
choices: Christ was always equal to the Father in every attribute from eternity and never grew or progressed in any way
Jesus 'received not of the fulness at the first, but continued from grace to grace until he received a fulness'; and worshippers can likewise advance grace to grace
Christ earned His divinity entirely by His own merit, independent of the Father, becoming a self-made God
Jesus only appeared to grow for our benefit, but in reality no real progression occurred in Him
source: Doctrine and Covenants 93:11-20
notes: A is the creedal 'immutable, eternally equal' Christology that denies any progression (protestant_trap). C makes the Son a self-made deity independent of the Father, a distortion of LDS teaching which keeps the Son subordinate to and dependent on the Father (progressive_trap). D treats the growth as mere appearance/docetism (plausible_near_miss). B is correct, quoting D&C 93:12-13, 19-20 — Christ progressed 'from grace to grace,' and the pattern is held out to disciples. Tests the distinctive LDS doctrine of divine progression as taught in D&C 93, contrasted with classical immutability.

question: Nephi writes that we are saved 'by grace, after all we can do' (2 Nephi 25:23). How does mainstream Latter-day Saint teaching now interpret this relationship between grace and works?
choices: Works earn salvation, and grace is only a small bonus God adds once a person has done enough good deeds to deserve it
Grace is sufficient by itself the moment one professes faith, so works are irrelevant evidence and add nothing to salvation
Salvation is a gift of grace made possible wholly by Christ's Atonement; our works and covenant faithfulness are how we receive and access that grace, not the price that purchases it
Grace and works each save about half, so a person must contribute fifty percent of the effort to be redeemed
source: 2 Nephi 25:23; Moroni 10:32-33; Doctrine and Covenants 138; "His Grace Is Sufficient" (Brad Wilcox, 2011); Gospel Topics: Grace
notes: A is the works-righteousness misreading where grace merely tops off human merit (correlation_oversimplification, the common members' over-literal reading of 'after all we can do'). B is grace-alone/faith-alone that dismisses works (protestant_trap). D is the folk 'we each do our 50%' arithmetic the Church has explicitly corrected (folk_doctrine_trap). C is correct: grace is the whole means of salvation, and obedience is how we lay hold on it — current teaching (e.g., Wilcox) clarifies 'after all we can do' as 'in addition to' rather than 'after we have earned our part.' Tests grasp of the corrected, mainstream grace/works synthesis rather than the old works-heavy folk reading.

question: Latter-day Saint doctrine teaches that God the Father has a body. Which statement most accurately states the official position and its scriptural basis?
choices: The Father is an incorporeal spirit 'without body, parts, or passions,' and references to His body are figurative anthropomorphisms
The Father has a glorified, perfected body of flesh and bones as tangible as man's; the Holy Ghost is a personage of spirit so that He can dwell in us
Only Christ has a body; the Father remains a formless spirit, and the Holy Ghost is merely an impersonal force or energy
The Father once had a body but laid it aside upon becoming God, returning to pure spirit
source: Doctrine and Covenants 130:22; Joseph Smith—History 1:17; Acts 7:55-56
notes: A is the Westminster Confession's incorporeal God 'without body, parts, or passions' (protestant_trap). C grants a body only to the Son and reduces the Holy Ghost to an impersonal force, mixing two errors (plausible_near_miss). D invents a 'laid aside His body' notion contrary to the doctrine of an eternal resurrected body (folk_doctrine_trap). B is correct (D&C 130:22): the Father and Son have bodies of flesh and bone, while the Holy Ghost is a personage of spirit. Tests the rejection of creedal divine incorporeality and the precise embodiment distinctions among the three members of the Godhead.

question: In Latter-day Saint theology, the phrase "the new and everlasting covenant" (D&C 132) is most precisely understood as referring to what?
choices: The specific practice of plural marriage as revealed to Joseph Smith, now suspended
The covenant of grace by which believers are justified through faith, renewed each Sabbath
The fulness of the gospel — the totality of gospel covenants and ordinances — within which celestial marriage stands as the crowning ordinance
The temple marriage ceremony itself, considered as a discrete ordinance separate from baptism and the endowment
source: D&C 132:6–7; 131:1–4; Gospel Topics, 'The New and Everlasting Covenant'
notes: Tests whether the model grasps that the 'new and everlasting covenant' is the entire restored gospel covenant system (D&C 132:6), of which eternal marriage is the highest ordinance — not a synonym for plural marriage (a common folk/anti-Mormon conflation since D&C 132 also discusses plural marriage), nor the Protestant covenant of grace, nor merely the wedding rite. Distinguishes conceptual understanding from keyword matching on 'covenant.'

question: How does The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995) characterize gender?
choices: Gender is a mortal condition that will be transcended and made irrelevant in the resurrection
Gender is an essential characteristic of individual premortal, mortal, and eternal identity and purpose
Gender is conferred at the Final Judgment according to one's faithfulness in mortality
The Proclamation affirms gender as essential in mortality but is deliberately silent regarding premortal existence
source: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995)
notes: The Proclamation's exact claim is that gender is essential to premortal, mortal, AND eternal identity — a strong continuity doctrine. The progressive distractor reverses this (gender as mortal/transcended); the near-miss truncates it by denying the premortal claim the text explicitly makes. Tests precise recall of doctrinal scope, not just the slogan.

question: The Family Proclamation outlines parental responsibilities. Which statement best captures its actual teaching on the relationship between those roles?
choices: Because the father holds the priesthood, he possesses final decision-making authority over his wife and household
Fathers and mothers fulfill fully interchangeable roles with no divinely appointed distinction between them
Fathers are to preside, provide, and protect, mothers are primarily responsible to nurture, and in these responsibilities they are obligated to help one another as equal partners
The husband presides in spiritual matters while the wife independently governs all temporal and domestic decisions
source: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995)
notes: The Proclamation pairs differentiated roles (preside/provide/protect vs. nurture) WITH the qualifier 'equal partners' and 'adapt' clauses — a both/and that resists both patriarchal overreach (priesthood = authority over wife, a folk reading) and the egalitarian erasure of role distinctions. The near-miss invents a false spiritual/temporal division. Tests the nuanced equal-partnership doctrine.

question: What does the Church teach about the spiritual status of a deceased person for whom vicarious temple ordinances (e.g., baptism for the dead) have been performed?
choices: The ordinance is offered on the person's behalf, but the deceased retains agency in the spirit world to accept or reject it
The ordinance automatically makes the deceased a member of the Church, regardless of that person's will
Only those who lived righteously in mortality can benefit; the wicked are excluded from receiving vicarious work
The proxy's faith completes the deceased's justification, securing their salvation by substitution
source: 1 Cor 15:29; D&C 138:31–34, 58; Gospel Topics, 'Baptisms for the Dead'
notes: Core doctrine: vicarious ordinances are invitations, not coercion — the dead exercise agency (D&C 138). The anti-Mormon distractor frames it as forced posthumous conversion (a recurring criticism); the correlation distractor wrongly limits the work to the righteous (the gospel is preached to ALL in spirit prison); the Protestant distractor imports proxy-faith justification. Tests agency-centered understanding.

question: In Latter-day Saint doctrine, what does 'eternal increase' (or a 'continuation of the seeds forever') denote as a blessing of the highest degree of the celestial kingdom?
choices: Becoming a ministering angel who serves separately and singly in God's presence forever
Being absorbed into the divine essence of God, no longer existing as a distinct individual
An ever-expanding fulness of knowledge and glory, understood figuratively rather than as literal posterity
A literal eternal posterity — the capacity, with one's spouse, to bear spirit offspring and become like one's Heavenly Parents
source: D&C 132:19–20, 30; 131:1–4; Gospel Topics, 'Becoming Like God'
notes: Eternal increase is literal — exalted couples receive 'a continuation of the seeds forever' (D&C 132:19). The near-miss assigns the fate of the UNexalted (ministering angels 'separately and singly,' D&C 132:16–17) to the exalted; the Protestant distractor imports Eastern-style absorption (loss of individuality); the correlation distractor spiritualizes 'increase' into mere knowledge. Tests literal exaltation/eternal-family doctrine vs. softened readings.

question: A child is born to a husband and wife who were previously sealed in the temple. What is this child's sealing status?
choices: The child must still receive a separate temple sealing-to-parents ordinance after birth to be bound to the family
The child is 'born in the covenant' and is automatically an heir to the blessings of the parents' sealing, requiring no additional sealing ordinance
Being born in the covenant guarantees the child's exaltation irrespective of the child's own future righteousness
The child is sealed to the parents only after being baptized at age eight
source: D&C 132:19; General Handbook 38.4 (Sealing); 'born in the covenant'
notes: Children of sealed parents are 'born in the covenant' (BIC) and need no separate sealing — distinguishing them from children sealed TO parents after the fact. The folk distractor inflates BIC into unconditional exaltation (the blessings remain contingent on covenant faithfulness); the near-misses invent unnecessary post-birth or post-baptism sealings. Tests the BIC vs. sealed-to-parents distinction.

question: What is the official position regarding faithful, covenant-keeping members who, through no fault of their own, do not marry or are not sealed in this life?
choices: No blessing — including exaltation — will ultimately be withheld from those who remain faithful to their covenants, though full receipt may come in the Lord's own time, including in the life to come
They may inherit the celestial kingdom as ministering servants but cannot receive exaltation, since that requires marriage in mortality
Their unmarried state reflects insufficient faith, and exaltation requires temple marriage during mortal life
The Church teaches such individuals can be exalted as autonomous individuals, since eternal marriage is not actually required for the highest glory
source: Dallin H. Oaks & Russell M. Nelson, Gen. Conf. addresses; General Handbook 38.5; D&C 137:7–9
notes: Official teaching reassures the faithful single that no blessing is permanently lost — eternal marriage remains essential to exaltation, but its receipt is not foreclosed by mortal circumstance and can come in eternity. The near-miss applies the unexalted 'ministering servant' fate to the involuntarily single; the folk distractor blames their faith; the progressive distractor denies marriage's necessity altogether. Tests the both/and: marriage required AND no faithful person ultimately denied.

question: According to Latter-day Saint doctrine, what makes a marriage able to continue beyond death and into eternity?
choices: A civil marriage performed by any legally authorized officiant, since love endures forever
Being sealed by the priesthood authority in a temple, with the ordinance ratified by the Holy Spirit of Promise
Simply being faithful and devoted to one's spouse throughout mortal life
A church wedding accompanied by sincere vows made in the name of Jesus Christ
source: D&C 132:7,19; Gospel Topics, 'Temples'
notes: Tests whether the model understands that eternal marriage requires sealing authority and the binding/sealing power (Holy Spirit of Promise), not mere love, sincerity, or a generic religious ceremony. The protestant_trap assumes any heartfelt marriage endures; correlation_oversimplification reduces it to devotion.

question: In 'The Family: A Proclamation to the World,' how is the family described in relation to God's plan?
choices: As a wonderful social institution that wise societies have always valued for stability
As central to the Creator's plan for the eternal destiny of His children
As one good lifestyle choice among several equally valid ways to find happiness
As primarily a means of teaching morality and passing on religious tradition
source: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995)
notes: The Proclamation states the family is 'central to the Creator's plan for the eternal destiny of His children.' Distractors swap eternal centrality for merely social/moral value (oversimplification) or relativize it (progressive_trap), testing grasp of the doctrine's eternal scope.

question: How does the Family Proclamation describe the roles of fathers and mothers in the home?
choices: Mothers preside and provide while fathers nurture, reflecting natural gender strengths
Fathers preside and provide, mothers nurture, and they are obligated to help one another as equal partners
Roles are entirely interchangeable, so couples should divide all duties identically
The father alone bears responsibility for the family while the mother submits to his authority
source: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995)
notes: The Proclamation assigns fathers to preside and provide, mothers to nurture, while affirming 'equal partners' and mutual help (with adaptation for individual circumstance). The anti_mormon_trap distorts it into female submission; the progressive_trap erases roles entirely; the near_miss reverses the roles.

question: Why do Latter-day Saints perform baptisms and other ordinances for the dead in temples?
choices: To pray the deceased out of purgatory and into heaven through the merits of the living
Because saving ordinances are essential for all, and the deceased who did not receive them can accept this vicarious work in the spirit world
To guarantee that every named ancestor is automatically saved regardless of their own choices
Because only those who hear the gospel in mortality can be saved, so the dead must be reached quickly
source: 1 Cor 15:29; D&C 128; Gospel Topics, 'Baptisms for the Dead'
notes: Tests understanding that the ordinance is offered vicariously and must be accepted by the deceased's agency in the spirit world—not automatic salvation (folk_doctrine_trap) nor a purgatory release (protestant_trap).

question: What is the Latter-day Saint understanding of 'eternal increase' promised to those who attain exaltation?
choices: The accumulation of greater knowledge and heavenly mansions as eternal rewards
A continuation of the family unit and the capacity to bear spirit children, becoming like our Heavenly Parents
Ruling over one's own planet as an entirely independent god, separate from God the Father
An ever-expanding circle of friends and loved ones reunited in a single undivided heaven
source: D&C 132:19-20; Gospel Topics, 'Becoming Like God'
notes: Eternal increase = continuation of the family/seeds and becoming like Heavenly Parents. The folk_doctrine_trap is the 'own planet, independent god' caricature; the near_miss substitutes generic rewards for eternal posterity.

question: What is taught about children born to parents who are sealed in the temple?
choices: They must be re-sealed to their parents as infants in a separate temple ceremony
They are 'born in the covenant'—already part of the eternal sealing of their parents
They are sealed to their parents only after being baptized at age eight
They inherit exaltation automatically and cannot lose their place in the family
source: Gospel Topics, 'Sealing'; General Handbook 27.3
notes: Children of sealed parents are 'born in the covenant' with no separate sealing needed; tests this vs. confusing it with the sealing of children to parents (for the not-yet-sealed) and vs. the folk idea of guaranteed exaltation regardless of agency.

question: What does the Church teach regarding a faithful member who, through no fault of their own, never has the opportunity to marry in this life?
choices: They are assigned to the terrestrial kingdom, since the celestial kingdom requires marriage
No blessing will be withheld from them; the Lord will provide every promised opportunity to those who remain faithful
They should lower their standards and marry outside the temple to avoid losing exaltation
Their salvation is secure, but they can only become ministering angels, never gods
source: The Family: A Proclamation; M. Russell Ballard, 'Hope in Christ'; General Handbook 38.5
notes: Official teaching: faithful members denied marriage in mortality lose no eternal blessing. Folk_doctrine_trap (auto-terrestrial) and the near_miss (only ministering angels, conflating with D&C 132's unmarried) test understanding of mercy/timing in the plan.

question: Why does the Church encourage members to research their family history and identify ancestors?
choices: So that living families can feel cultural pride in their heritage and lineage
To find ancestors so their temple ordinances can be performed, linking generations through sealing
Because tracing one's pedigree proves descent from the house of Israel for patriarchal blessings
To preserve genealogical records that would otherwise be lost to secular historians
source: Malachi 4:5-6; D&C 2; Gospel Topics, 'Family History Work'
notes: Family history exists to provide saving/sealing temple ordinances and turn hearts of children and fathers—not mainly heritage pride, lineage-proving, or record preservation. Tests the redemptive-temple purpose behind genealogy.

question: In Latter-day Saint doctrine, what is the relationship between exaltation in the celestial kingdom and eternal marriage?
choices: Eternal marriage is encouraged but a faithful individual can be exalted alone through personal righteousness
The new and everlasting covenant of marriage is required to receive the highest degree of the celestial kingdom
Marriage matters only in mortality; in the resurrection all relationships are equal as among the angels
Any worthy person reaches the celestial kingdom, and marriage merely adds extra glory there
notes: Exaltation (highest celestial degree) requires the new and everlasting covenant of marriage. The protestant_trap echoes 'neither marry nor are given in marriage'; the near_miss conflates entering the celestial kingdom with exaltation in its highest degree.

question: A faithful, temple-worthy member who keeps her covenants but never has the opportunity to marry in this life sometimes worries about exaltation. What does the Church officially teach about her eternal prospects?
choices: Because eternal marriage is required for exaltation and cannot be received here, she has missed her chance and can attain at most the terrestrial kingdom
No blessing, including eternal marriage and exaltation, will be withheld from those who remain faithful but are denied these opportunities through no fault of their own; the Lord will provide a way
Salvation is by grace alone, so marriage and sealing have no bearing on whether she is exalted
Exaltation is reserved for those married in this life, but she can still serve forever as a ministering angel in the celestial kingdom
source: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995); General Handbook 38.1; D&C 137:7-9; teachings that no blessing is withheld from the faithful who lack opportunity through no fault of their own
notes: Tests whether the model grasps the official compassionate teaching rather than a rigid Sunday-School syllogism. The first choice oversimplifies the 'marriage is required' rule into condemnation, ignoring the promise that opportunities denied in mortality will be extended in eternity. The grace-alone option is a protestant_trap denying the necessity of sealing ordinances. The 'ministering angel' option is a folk_doctrine_trap conflating the fate of those who reject the covenant (D&C 132:16-17) with that of the faithful who never had the chance. The keyed answer reflects the consistent First Presidency assurance that the faithful lose nothing eternally.

question: A devoted single sister lives and dies in full faithfulness but, through no fault of her own, never has the opportunity to be sealed in marriage during mortality. Which statement best reflects the official, correlated position on her eternal prospects?
choices: She is consigned to a lesser, ministering station in the terrestrial kingdom, since exaltation strictly requires that the sealing be contracted and lived during mortal life.

Latter-day prophets have repeatedly promised that no blessing — including eternal marriage and exaltation — will ultimately be withheld from those who faithfully desire it but are denied the opportunity in mortality through no fault of their own.
The marriage requirement for exaltation is largely a cultural overlay; worthy individuals are in fact exalted as individuals, and the sealing ideal is aspirational rather than necessary.
Because vicarious sealings cannot be performed for a person who died never married, her exaltation is doctrinally foreclosed regardless of her righteousness.
She remains an unexalted single being unless a future descendant arranges a proxy marriage sealing on her behalf, the absence of which permanently bars her progress.
source: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995); General Handbook 27.x; Russell M. Nelson and Dallin H. Oaks teachings on covenant blessings withheld from none who faithfully desire them
notes: Tests whether the model grasps the official 'no blessing withheld' promise (the mainstream pastoral position) rather than a legalistic timing requirement (A), a progressive denial that marriage matters for exaltation (B/progressive), or anti-Mormon/near-miss claims about vicarious sealing impossibility (D/E). Distinguishes understanding of conditional vs. unconditional eternal-family doctrine.

question: How does The Family: A Proclamation to the World frame the relationship between a father's responsibility to 'preside' and the spousal relationship as a whole?
choices: The terms 'preside,' 'provide,' and 'nurture' are illustrative metaphors carrying no normative weight; the roles are fully interchangeable by mutual preference.
The father's presiding role establishes a hierarchy of final decision in which the mother is to defer to his judgment when the partners disagree.

Fathers are to preside, provide, and protect while mothers are primarily responsible for nurture, yet in these sacred responsibilities the two are 'obligated to help one another as equal partners,' with adaptation permitted for individual circumstances.
Presiding belongs to the husband because he holds priesthood keys within the home over his wife and children, making his governance an extension of priesthood authority.
Nurturing is assigned exclusively to the mother and the document forbids fathers from serving as a child's primary caregiver under any circumstance.
source: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995), paragraph 7; Dallin H. Oaks, 'Priesthood Authority in the Family and the Church' (Oct 2005)
notes: The Proclamation's own text pairs 'preside/provide/nurture' WITH 'equal partners' and 'individual adaptation.' Tests whether the model holds both halves together against a progressive erasure of roles (A), the common folk reading of presiding as a chain-of-command/decisional veto (B), the folk error that a husband holds priesthood keys over his wife (D — Oaks explicitly denies keys are exercised over family members in this way), and an oversimplified exclusivity claim (E).

question: A child is 'born in the covenant' to parents already sealed in the temple, but later as an adult becomes inactive. Which statement most accurately captures the child's sealing status and its doctrinal conditions?
choices: The child must still receive a separate child-to-parent sealing ordinance to belong to the eternal family; being born in the covenant secures only mortal birth into the home.

Born in the covenant, the child is already an heir to the blessings of the parents' sealing without any additional sealing ordinance, though actually realizing those blessings remains conditioned upon the child's own faithfulness and covenant keeping.
Because the child was born in the covenant, exaltation is guaranteed unconditionally; once that status attaches, personal agency can no longer forfeit the promised blessing.
The parents' own exaltation and promised eternal increase are nullified if any of their sealed children prove unfaithful, since a broken family chain voids the parents' sealing.
'Born in the covenant' is an informal folk expression with no standing in the General Handbook and confers no ordinance-related status whatsoever.
source: General Handbook 38.x (sealing policies; 'born in the covenant'); D&C 132:19–20 (eternal increase); Boyd K. Packer and others on conditional sealing blessings
notes: Tests the nuanced BIC doctrine: no additional ordinance is needed (defeats A's near-miss), yet the blessing is conditional on the child's faithfulness (defeats C's unconditional folk view). Also probes whether the model wrongly thinks a child's apostasy voids the parents' exaltation/eternal increase (D oversimplification) or denies the term's official standing (E). Requires synthesis of sealing policy with the conditional nature of covenant promises.

question: In Latter-day Saint doctrine, what actually causes a temple marriage to endure beyond death into eternity?
choices: The depth of the couple's love, which by its very nature never ends
It is performed by one holding the sealing power and is ratified by the Holy Spirit of Promise
A legally binding civil contract solemnized within a sacred, dedicated space
The couple's continued mutual faithfulness alone, which keeps the bond intact
source: D&C 132:7,19; General Handbook 27.3; The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995)
notes: Tests whether the model grasps that eternal duration comes from authorized priesthood sealing AND ratification by the Holy Spirit of Promise—not sentiment (folk), legal form (near miss), or faithfulness as the binding mechanism (oversimplification). Faithfulness is required to retain blessings but is not what creates the eternal bond.

question: According to The Family: A Proclamation to the World, how is 'gender' characterized?
choices: A social construct shaped primarily by mortal culture and upbringing
An essential characteristic of individual premortal, mortal, and eternal identity and purpose
A mortal condition that will be removed and made irrelevant in the resurrection
A label assigned at birth that has no bearing on one's eternal state
source: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995), para. 2
notes: Discriminates the Proclamation's actual language ('essential characteristic of individual premortal, mortal, and eternal identity') from the heterodox social-construct reading (progressive) and the mistaken notion that gender is mortal-only and dissolves at resurrection (folk/near-miss).

question: How does the Proclamation describe the respective responsibilities of fathers and mothers?
choices: Fathers preside, provide, and protect; mothers are primarily responsible to nurture; and they are obligated to help one another as equal partners
Mothers must remain in the home at all times while fathers alone make every family decision
Parental roles are fully interchangeable with no divinely appointed distinction whatsoever
The father presides with final authority and the mother is to submit to him in all things
source: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995), para. 7
notes: Tests the nuance that the Proclamation pairs distinct primary responsibilities WITH 'equal partners' and 'adapt' clauses—rejecting both the rigid stay-home/patriarchal-authority caricature (oversimplification/anti-Mormon) and the no-distinction reading (progressive).

question: What did the keys restored by Elijah in the Kirtland Temple on April 3, 1836, make possible for the family?
choices: The keys of gathering scattered Israel from the four parts of the earth
The sealing power that binds families across generations and authorizes vicarious temple ordinances for the dead
Permission for departed ancestors to be saved without any earthly ordinances performed for them
Authority to translate ancient genealogical records by the gift and power of God
notes: Elijah restored the sealing keys; Moses restored the gathering keys in the same vision (near miss). Tests understanding that vicarious ordinances are still required—ancestors are not saved 'automatically' (folk)—and the keys are about sealing, not translation.

question: D&C 132 promises that those who attain the highest degree of celestial glory through the new and everlasting covenant will receive what blessing connected to eternal family?
choices: A continuation of the seeds, or eternal increase—the capacity to bear spirit offspring forever
Rest from all labor and creation, having finished their work in mortality
Ministering as angels to exalted beings throughout eternity
Absorption into the divine nature, surrendering their individual identity in God
source: D&C 132:19-20,22-24,30; Gospel Topics: Becoming Like God
notes: Eternal increase ('continuation of the seeds') is the keyed blessing. The 'ministering angels' option is what D&C 132:16-17 says happens to those who do NOT enter the covenant (near miss), and 'absorption into God' is the mystical-Christian view rejected by LDS theology (protestant).

question: What is the doctrinal status of a child whose parents were sealed in the temple before that child was born?
choices: Born in the covenant—already an heir to the blessings of the parents' sealing, with no separate sealing ordinance needed
Required to be sealed to the parents in a separate temple ordinance after being baptized
Guaranteed exaltation regardless of the choices he or she later makes in life
Considered sealed only once the child personally receives the temple endowment
source: General Handbook 27.4; Guide to the Scriptures, 'Born in the Covenant'
notes: 'Born in the covenant' children need no separate sealing—unlike children sealed to parents later (near miss). Tests that birth in the covenant confers heirship but not unconditional exaltation; agency and worthiness still govern outcomes (folk).

question: What does the Church officially teach concerning faithful members who, through no fault of their own, do not have the opportunity to marry in the temple during mortality?
choices: They are permanently excluded from the celestial kingdom because they lacked temple marriage
No blessing will be withheld from those who are worthy and faithful; the Lord will provide every opportunity in His own time
They automatically become ministering angels, since exaltation strictly requires marriage in this life
They will simply be assigned a spouse by Church leaders in the spirit world
source: General Handbook 38.1; Russell M. Nelson and Dallin H. Oaks counsel to single members; The Living Christ principles
notes: The official assurance is that the faithful lose no blessing in the eternities. Distractors include the hostile 'barred forever' claim (anti-Mormon), the misapplied 'become angels' reading of D&C 132:16 (folk), and the assigned-spouse folklore.

question: Why is celestial (temple) marriage considered essential in Latter-day Saint doctrine?
choices: Because the marriage ordinance itself remits the couple's sins at the altar
Because exaltation—the highest degree within the celestial kingdom—requires entering the new and everlasting covenant of marriage
Because it is the only means by which a person can be saved at all and escape eternal punishment
Because unmarried people cannot inherit any kingdom of glory in the next life
source: D&C 131:1-4; 132:19-21; Gospel Topics: 'Becoming Like God'
notes: Tests the precise claim: temple marriage is required for EXALTATION (highest celestial degree), not for general salvation or admission to a kingdom of glory. Distractors conflate exaltation with salvation/heaven (oversimplification, anti-Mormon) and invent a sin-remitting function (folk).

question: Which statement best reflects the Proclamation's teaching about marriage within the Creator's plan?
choices: Marriage between a man and a woman is ordained of God and central to His plan for the eternal destiny of His children
