Marriage is a wise social arrangement but is not essential to one's eternal salvation or progression
Any committed, loving partnership fulfills the Creator's plan for the family equally well
Marriage was instituted only after the Fall as a practical means to populate the earth
source: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995), para. 1,7
notes: Keys to the Proclamation's 'ordained of God...central to the Creator's plan.' Distractors include the heterodox 'optional/equivalent partnership' readings (progressive) and the historically mistaken 'marriage began after the Fall' claim—Adam and Eve were married before the Fall (near miss).

question: According to 'The Family: A Proclamation to the World,' how does it describe the relationship between a husband's and wife's roles in presiding over and providing for the family?
choices: The husband presides and provides while the wife's primary duty is silent submission, as the order is fixed and unequal
Fathers preside and provide and mothers nurture, yet they are 'obligated to help one another as equal partners,' with adaptation allowed for individual circumstances
Roles are entirely interchangeable social constructs that the Proclamation leaves to each couple's preference
The wife presides spiritually while the husband presides temporally, dividing authority between two separate spheres
source: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995)
notes: The Proclamation pairs 'preside/provide' (father) and 'nurture' (mother) but explicitly says they are 'equal partners' and that 'disability, death, or other circumstances may necessitate individual adaptation.' The folk distractor exaggerates patriarchy into 'silent submission'; the progressive distractor erases the stated roles entirely; the near-miss invents a temporal/spiritual split. Tests whether a model holds the proclamation's both/and (defined roles AND equal partnership) rather than collapsing to one pole.

question: A faithful Latter-day Saint woman never marries in mortality through no fault of her own. What is the official teaching about her eternal prospects?
choices: Because eternal marriage is required for exaltation, she is permanently barred from the highest degree and will minister as an angel forever
No blessing will be withheld from a faithful person; the Lord will provide every promised blessing, including eternal marriage, in His own time and way
She automatically receives exaltation as a single person, since marriage is optional for those who keep their covenants
She must be sealed as a plural wife to a worthy man in the next life to qualify for the celestial kingdom
source: General Handbook 27.4; teachings of the First Presidency on faithful members who do not marry in mortality
notes: Official teaching: ordinances/blessings unavailable through no fault of one's own will be provided; no blessing is lost to the faithful. The oversimplified distractor draws a rigid 'no temple marriage = no exaltation, forever' from the doctrine that marriage IS required, ignoring that mortality isn't the deadline. The progressive distractor makes marriage optional; the folk distractor revives plural-marriage-in-heaven speculation. Tests understanding that the marriage requirement is real but timing extends beyond this life.

question: Why does the Church emphasize members doing their own family history research before performing temple ordinances for the dead?
choices: Because vicarious ordinances are invalid unless performed by a blood relative of the deceased
Because the work binds the hearts of the living to their ancestors and offers saving ordinances the deceased may accept or reject in the spirit world
Because the dead cannot be saved at all without descendants who personally locate their names
Because completing the family chart is a worthiness requirement for entering the temple
source: D&C 128; Malachi 4:5-6; 1 Cor 15:29; Gospel Topics, 'Family History and Temple Work'
notes: Family history work turns hearts (Malachi/Elijah) and provides ordinances the dead can accept by agency; it is not restricted to blood relatives, and the deceased's salvation does not depend on descendants. The folk distractor over-literalizes the encouragement to seek one's own kindred; the anti-mormon distractor frames the dead as helpless hostages; the near-miss confuses family history with a temple-recommend requirement. Tests grasp of agency-in-the-spirit-world and vicarious ordinance theology.

question: What is the official understanding of 'eternal increase' or 'eternal lives' promised to those who attain the highest degree of the celestial kingdom?
choices: The continuation of the family unit and the seeds (posterity) forever, so that the exalted become 'gods' inheriting all the Father has
A symbolic, non-literal expansion of love and influence with no actual continuation of family relationships
Reincarnation through successive mortal probations on other worlds until perfection is reached
Reigning over one's own newly created planet, which is the central scriptural definition of exaltation
source: D&C 131:1-4; D&C 132:19-20; Gospel Topics Essay, 'Becoming Like God'
notes: Exaltation includes 'a continuation of the seeds forever' and inheriting all the Father has (D&C 132); the sealed family persists and the exalted become like God. The progressive distractor strips the literalness; the anti-mormon distractor inserts reincarnation (not LDS doctrine); the folk distractor reduces it to the 'own planet' caricature the Church does not teach as the definition. Tests literal-family-continuation vs. both deflationary and caricatured readings.

question: A member reasons that because D&C 89 prohibits only "hot drinks," iced black tea and cold-brewed green tea are acceptable. According to the Church's 2019 clarification, what is the correct understanding?
choices: "Hot drinks" has been authoritatively interpreted by the Brethren as coffee and tea, and because green and black tea both come from the same tea plant, both are prohibited regardless of serving temperature.
Temperature is the operative factor in the revelation, so chilled or iced versions of these beverages fall outside the prohibition.
Only black tea is prohibited; green tea is treated as a permitted health drink alongside herbal teas.
Since the Word of Wisdom was given "not by commandment," these beverages are simply matters of individual conscience with no Church standard attached.
source: Newsroom, "Statement on the Word of Wisdom," Aug 2019; D&C 89:9
notes: Tests whether the model grasps that the prohibition keys on the tea plant (Camellia sinensis), not temperature or color. B exploits the literal 'hot' wording; C is a common member misbelief; D weaponizes D&C 89:2's preface ('not by commandment') as a modern opt-out, ignoring that it is now a temple-recommend standard.

question: How does the Church currently define the tithe a member is asked to pay?
choices: One-tenth of one's income or increase, with the determination of what constitutes 'income' left to the individual member between themselves and the Lord.
One-tenth of net income only, calculated after taxes and necessary living expenses, per established Church policy.
One-tenth of the surplus or savings remaining at year's end, consistent with the original 1838 standard still in force today.
A freewill offering of whatever percentage one feels spiritually prompted to give in a given year.
source: D&C 119:4; General Handbook 34.3.1; First Presidency statement on tithing (1970)
notes: The official definition is deliberately principle-based ('income/increase'), explicitly leaving gross-vs-net to the individual. B reflects a widespread folk assumption that net is mandated; C conflates the early 1838 'surplus property' phase (Edward Partridge era) with current practice; D dissolves the fixed tenth into discretionary giving. Tests doctrinal-development awareness.

question: Which statement best reflects the Church's teaching about who should partake of the sacrament?
choices: The sacrament renews covenants and conveys the cleansing power of the Atonement; members troubled by ordinary failings are encouraged to partake, though a bishop may counsel one guilty of serious sin to refrain for a season.
Only members who are fully worthy and hold a current temple recommend should partake.
Anyone who has committed any sin during the week must abstain until repentance for it is complete.
It is a symbolic remembrance carrying no covenantal renewal, so partaking is an optional act of personal expression.
source: General Handbook 18.9; Moroni 6:6; 3 Nephi 18; teachings of D. Todd Christofferson on the sacrament
notes: Tests understanding that the sacrament is a means of grace and renewal, not a reward for the perfect. B imports temple-worthiness as the bar (it is not); C is the legalistic 'unworthy = abstain' oversimplification many members hold; D strips the ordinance of its covenant function. The nuance—bishop's counsel only in serious cases—is the discriminator.

question: Ministering, introduced in April 2018, replaced home teaching and visiting teaching. Which description most accurately captures how it differs?
choices: It emphasizes flexible, needs-centered care rather than a required monthly visit with a prepared lesson; ministering interviews occur quarterly, and young women ages 14–18 may serve as companions, paralleling young men.
It is essentially renamed home teaching, retaining the monthly in-home visit, a correlated monthly message, and monthly reporting.
It eliminated all leadership oversight and reporting, making care purely informal with no accountability to elders quorum or Relief Society presidencies.
It transferred watchcare from local lay members to a stake-level professional social-services corps.
source: General Handbook 21.1–21.3; April 2018 general conference ministering announcements
notes: Discriminates real structural change (flexibility, quarterly interviews, YW 14–18 as companions) from cosmetic relabeling (B). C overstates the loss of accountability—interviews and assignment-tracking remain; D invents a professionalization the Church explicitly rejects in favor of lay watchcare.

question: According to the Church's principles of welfare and self-reliance, what is the proper order for meeting a member's temporal needs?
choices: Individuals provide for themselves to the extent they can; family assists next; the Church, through the bishop and fast offerings, helps when individual and family resources are insufficient.
Members should turn first to the bishops' storehouse, since caring for the poor is principally the Church's institutional responsibility.
Public and government assistance should be exhausted first, with Church help reserved as a final resort.
True self-reliance requires declining all outside aid, including from family and the Church, as a matter of gospel principle.
source: General Handbook 22.1–22.3; "Providing in the Lord's Way" welfare principles
notes: Tests the self–family–Church sequence. B is the common folk inversion (Church first); C plausibly reorders to government-first, which the Church neither mandates nor forbids but does not place first; D caricatures self-reliance as isolationist, missing that interdependence and accepting help when needed are part of the doctrine.

question: D&C 9, addressed to Oliver Cowdery, describes how personal revelation is typically received. Which best states its teaching?
choices: One must first study the matter out in the mind and reach a decision, then ask God for confirmation; a burning in the bosom confirms a right course, while a 'stupor of thought' signals a wrong one.
One should quiet and empty the mind and wait passively for a feeling of warmth, without first reasoning toward a conclusion.
Personal revelation on important matters comes only through priesthood channels, requiring a leader's confirmation rather than an individual's.
Because spiritual feelings are unreliable, decisions should rest on reason and evidence rather than on seeking divine confirmation.
notes: Tests grasp of the study-then-confirm pattern central to LDS epistemology. B is the passive 'wait for a feeling' oversimplification that omits the required mental labor; C misapplies priesthood-channel doctrine to personal revelation; D is the rationalist dismissal of spiritual confirmation altogether.

question: Paul distinguishes 'godly sorrow' from 'the sorrow of the world' (2 Corinthians 7:10), a contrast President Russell M. Nelson echoed in teaching that repentance is positive. Which best captures the doctrine?
choices: Godly sorrow is a Spirit-prompted desire to change and turn to God that 'worketh repentance to salvation,' whereas worldly sorrow is mere regret over consequences or being caught; repentance itself is a hopeful change of heart and mind, not a punishment.
Godly sorrow means feeling enough guilt and self-imposed suffering to prove to God that one merits forgiveness.
Repentance is earning forgiveness through compensating works, since grace covers only what human effort cannot reach.
Because Christ's grace is unconditional, sorrow for sin is unnecessary; one simply accepts a forgiveness already fully granted.
source: 2 Corinthians 7:9–10; Russell M. Nelson, "We Can Do Better and Be Better," Apr 2019
notes: Tests whether repentance is understood as joyful change (metanoia) flowing from godly sorrow, not penance. B is the 'suffer enough to earn it' caricature; C is the anti-Mormon 'works-righteousness' framing; D is the cheap-grace Protestant trap that erases the need for sorrow and change.

question: A new member notices green tea is sold as a health drink and asks whether it falls under the Word of Wisdom. Based on the Church's 2019 clarification, what is the correct answer?
choices: Green tea is acceptable; only black tea is prohibited as a 'hot drink.'
Both green and black tea are prohibited, because they come from the same tea plant.
All warm beverages are forbidden, so even herbal teas violate the Word of Wisdom.
It is entirely a matter of personal conscience, with no official guidance.
source: Newsroom, 'Statement on the Word of Wisdom,' Aug 2019; D&C 89
notes: Tests whether the model knows the 2019 clarification that 'tea from the tea plant — green AND black' is prohibited (same Camellia plant), while herbal teas are not. Distractors include the common folk belief that only black/dark tea counts and the over-broad reading that bans all warm drinks.

question: In Latter-day Saint practice, what is the central purpose of partaking of the sacrament during sacrament meeting?
choices: To renew the covenants made at baptism and to remember Jesus Christ and His Atonement.
To effect a change in which the bread and water become the literal body and blood of Christ.
To reward those who are already sinless; only the fully worthy and perfect may partake.
To satisfy a required checklist item for the temple recommend interview.
source: D&C 20:75-79; Moroni 4-5; Gospel Topics, 'Sacrament'
notes: Tests understanding that the sacrament renews baptismal covenants and centers on remembering Christ—not transubstantiation (Catholic trap) and not a reward limited to the 'perfect' (folk trap that discourages humble participation).

question: How does the Church define the law of tithing?
choices: A voluntary monthly donation of whatever amount one can comfortably afford.
One-tenth of one's increase (income), with the member determining what constitutes increase.
Exactly ten percent of gross pay, mandated and audited by the bishop each year.
An Old Testament ordinance fulfilled in Christ and no longer required of believers.
source: D&C 119; Gospel Topics, 'Tithing'
notes: Tests the precise teaching: one-tenth of increase, with members privately deciding how to compute it. Distractors include the casual 'give what you can' view, the bishop-audited rigid version, and the Protestant 'tithing is fulfilled/abolished' framing.

question: What does the Church teach about proper fasting and the fast offering?
choices: Going without food and water—usually for two consecutive meals—with prayer, donating at least the value of the meals as a fast offering.
Strict abstention from all food and water for a full 24 hours, or the fast does not count.
A symbolic gesture only; simply eating a smaller meal fulfills the law of the fast.
Fast offerings substitute for tithing among members with low incomes.
source: Isaiah 58; General Handbook 22.2; 'The Law of the Fast'
notes: Tests the standard teaching: abstaining about two meals plus a generous fast offering. The 24-hour rigid version is a common folk overstatement; tithing and fast offerings are distinct contributions.

question: According to Church teaching, who has the responsibility to share the gospel?
choices: Only full-time, set-apart missionaries serving in the field.
Every member of the Church is invited and responsible to share the gospel.
Only the bishop and the ward mission leader.
No one should actively share, since inviting others can be coercive.
source: D&C 88:81; Preach My Gospel; 'Every Member a Missionary'
notes: Tests the 'every member a missionary' principle versus the narrowing of missionary duty to full-time elders/sisters or ward leaders, and versus the heterodox view that sharing faith is inherently coercive.

question: In April 2018, the Church introduced 'ministering.' What did it replace, and how does it function?
choices: It replaced home teaching and visiting teaching with flexible care and quarterly ministering interviews.
It replaced them with a required monthly visit accompanied by a standardized prepared lesson.
It assigned all fellowshipping responsibility exclusively to the full-time missionaries.
It taught that members minister only within their own immediate families.
source: Newsroom, April 2018 general conference announcements; General Handbook 21.1
notes: Tests knowledge that ministering replaced home/visiting teaching and is intentionally flexible with quarterly interviews—not the old rigid monthly-lesson model it replaced (the plausible near-miss describes the former system).

question: What is the proper order of resources taught in the Church's principles of self-reliance and welfare?
choices: Rely first on government programs, turning to family and the Church only afterward.
Rely first on one's own efforts and family, then on the Church, with work as a governing principle.
Rely on faith alone, since temporal preparation shows a lack of trust in God.
Depend on the bishops' storehouse as an ongoing, permanent source of support.
source: General Handbook 22; 'Providing in the Lord's Way'; Self-Reliance materials
notes: Tests the welfare principle of self-reliance: individual and family first, then the Church, with work emphasized. Distractors invert the order, spiritualize away preparation, or treat Church assistance as permanent rather than temporary.

question: According to D&C 9, how does the Lord teach us to seek and recognize personal revelation in our decisions?
choices: We wait passively until a strong feeling arrives without any effort on our part.
We study it out in our own minds, reach a decision, then ask God to confirm it—a peaceful/burning feeling confirms, a stupor of thought warns against it.
Personal revelation is merely emotion and has no real doctrinal foundation.
Only prophets receive revelation; members should simply follow leaders without seeking personal confirmation.
notes: Tests the active model of revelation—study it out, decide, then seek confirmation—versus the passive 'just wait for a feeling' caricature, the dismissive 'it's only emotion' view, and the folk notion that members shouldn't seek their own revelation.

question: What is the central emphasis of the 'Come, Follow Me' program introduced in 2019?
choices: Home-centered and Church-supported gospel study and learning.
Eliminating Church meetings entirely in favor of study done only at home.
Unstructured independent study with no curriculum, members choosing any topic they like.
Study directed exclusively by Sunday School teachers during the Sunday block.
source: Come, Follow Me—For Individuals and Families; Jan 2019 two-hour block announcement
notes: Tests the defining phrase 'home-centered, Church-supported.' Distractors exaggerate it into home-only (eliminating church), strip it of curriculum, or wrongly keep it teacher-centered at church—each missing the balanced model.

question: A new member asks whether green tea is acceptable under the Word of Wisdom, since it's marketed as a healthy 'herbal' drink. What is the Church's clarified position (per the 2019 New Era statement)?
choices: Green tea is fine because the prohibition on 'hot drinks' refers only to black coffee and black tea, not lighter varieties
Green tea is prohibited because it comes from the same tea plant as black tea, and both green and black tea are off-limits
Green tea is a matter of personal conscience; the Word of Wisdom only bans alcohol, tobacco, and coffee by name
Green tea is acceptable as long as it is served cold or iced rather than hot, since the rule targets 'hot drinks'
source: Newsroom, 'Statement on the Word of Wisdom,' New Era, Aug 2019; D&C 89
notes: Tests whether the model grasps that the prohibition tracks the tea plant (Camellia sinensis), so green AND black tea are both prohibited. The temperature distractor exploits the literal 'hot drinks' wording (folk legalism) — but iced tea is still tea; the 'only named substances' distractor is the permissive Sunstone reading; the 'lighter varieties' option is a near-miss that gets the same-plant logic backwards.

question: In Latter-day Saint practice, what is the basic relationship between tithing and the fast offering?
choices: The fast offering is simply the portion of one's tithing set aside specifically to feed the poor in the ward
Tithing is one-tenth of one's increase paid to the Church; the fast offering is a separate, additional donation—ideally at least the cost of the meals skipped while fasting—used to care for the needy
Both are voluntary suggestions; faithful members may fulfill the obligation by donating either ten percent OR a fast offering, whichever they can afford
Tithing fulfills the law of sacrifice, so members who pay a full tithe are not expected to also contribute fast offerings
source: General Handbook 34.3.1–34.4; Isaiah 58; D&C 119
notes: Tests understanding that tithing (10% of increase) and the fast offering (a distinct donation tied to monthly fasting, traditionally the value of the meals missed, devoted to the poor) are two separate principles, not interchangeable. The first distractor collapses them into one fund (oversimplification); the third treats them as either/or (heterodox/permissive); the fourth invents an exemption that sounds doctrinally tidy but is false.

question: A high priest argues that since the 2019 New Era clarification names coffee and tea by the plant, the underlying offense of the 'hot drinks' provision must really be caffeine, and that energy drinks and caffeinated cola are therefore against the Word of Wisdom. How does this reasoning compare with the Church's official position?
choices: It is correct: the Church teaches that caffeine is the prohibited substance, so all caffeinated beverages violate the Word of Wisdom.

It is mistaken: the clarification prohibits coffee and all tea from the tea plant (green and black) by name, and the Church has explicitly stated the Word of Wisdom does not mention caffeine and does not prohibit other caffeinated drinks, leaving those to individual judgment.
It is mistaken in detail but right in spirit: caffeine is officially 'strongly discouraged' though not formally forbidden, so cola is a lesser violation than coffee.
It is correct only for hot caffeinated drinks, since 'hot drinks' refers to temperature, making iced coffee and iced tea acceptable.
source: Newsroom, 'Statement on the Word of Wisdom,' Aug 2019; D&C 89; Newsroom statement clarifying caffeine is not specified
notes: Tests whether the model grasps that 'hot drinks' was authoritatively defined as coffee and tea (the plant, not temperature, not caffeine). The caffeine theory is a pervasive folk reading; the Church has said the revelation does not mention caffeine. Distractor D weaponizes the literal word 'hot' as a temperature trap, which the green-AND-black-tea clarification refutes.

question: A member preparing a lesson asks how a proper fast offering relates to the law of the fast. Which statement best captures the Church's teaching on the amount and purpose?
choices: Members donate exactly the retail cost of the meals skipped, which the bishop forwards directly to the specific poor families in the ward.

Members abstain from two meals and contribute at minimum the value of the food not eaten—generously, even far more—to bishops' storehouse welfare funds the bishop administers to care for the poor and needy.
Fast offerings are a fixed second tithe (a tenth beyond regular tithing) required for a temple recommend.
Fasting is the essential commandment; the monetary offering is a cultural Utah practice and is optional in the broader Church.
source: General Handbook 22.2; Isaiah 58; Malachi 3; M. Russell Ballard teachings on generous fast offerings
notes: Tests synthesis of the law of the fast: abstain two meals, give at least their value (ideally generously), administered through the bishop's welfare funds. Distractor A traps the literalist 'exact cost / direct to named family' misunderstanding; C confuses fast offerings with a tithe-like temple-recommend requirement; D is the heterodox dismissal of the offering as mere regional custom.

question: In the ministering program announced in 2018, an elders quorum president wonders how to evaluate whether companionships are succeeding. Which approach best reflects the program's design and intent?
choices: Count completed monthly in-home visits with a prepared lesson, the metric that home teaching always used.

Focus on whether real needs are being met and people are cared for in the Savior's way—using flexible methods (visits, calls, texts, service)—and account for it through quarterly ministering interviews rather than a monthly visit tally.
Require a signed monthly report from each companionship and read the percentages over the pulpit to motivate improvement.
Treat ministering as wholly informal with no reporting, since assigning people to families contradicts the spirit of charity.
source: General Handbook 21.1–21.3; April 2018 general conference (ministering announcements); quarterly ministering interviews
notes: Tests understanding that ministering deliberately replaced the monthly-visit-with-lesson model with needs-focused flexibility accounted through quarterly interviews. Distractor A imports the old home-teaching metric; C is the common practice the change was meant to end; D over-corrects into a heterodox 'no structure at all' reading that ignores the retained interview/accountability framework.

question: A returned missionary studying D&C 9 concludes that the 'burning in the bosom' means a believer should expect a warm emotional confirmation before acting, and that absence of such a feeling means God has said no. How does this square with the section's actual counsel on personal revelation?
choices: It is accurate: revelation comes as a distinct warm feeling, and its absence is itself the 'stupor of thought' signifying a denial.

It oversimplifies: D&C 9 teaches one must first 'study it out' and reach a decision, then ask for confirmation; a 'burning' or 'good' feeling confirms while a 'stupor of thought' warns—revelation requires effort and is often quiet, not merely an emotional glow.
It is mistaken: personal revelation is purely intellectual reasoning, and the 'burning' language is figurative for a logically sound conclusion.
It is correct in principle, but such confirmations are reserved for prophets; ordinary members should follow leaders rather than seek personal revelation on their own decisions.
source: D&C 9:7–9; Moroni 10:3–5; teachings on personal revelation (e.g., Bednar, 'Patterns of Light')
notes: Tests whether the model grasps the full D&C 9 pattern—study it out, decide, then seek confirmation—rather than reducing revelation to an automatic emotional thermometer. Distractor A is the folk 'feelings only' reading; C is the rationalist over-correction denying spiritual feeling; D is the false notion that lay members shouldn't seek revelation for personal choices, contradicting the doctrine of universal personal revelation.

question: A recent convert notes that the Word of Wisdom mentions only "hot drinks" and asks whether green tea and iced tea are therefore acceptable. What is the Church's official clarification?
choices: Green tea is fine; only black tea counts as a forbidden "hot drink"
All tea brewed from the tea plant (Camellia sinensis) — green and black alike — is prohibited, hot or iced
Any caffeinated beverage, including cola and energy drinks, is forbidden under this rule
Tea is acceptable when served cold, since the prohibition applies only to drinks consumed hot
source: Newsroom, "Statement on the Word of Wisdom," Aug 2019; D&C 89
notes: The 2019 clarification keys to the source plant, not color or temperature. Distractor A and D fixate on the literal 'hot drinks'/'black tea' wording (plausible near miss); C reflects the widespread folk belief equating caffeine itself with the prohibition. Tests whether a model grasps that 'tea' = the tea plant, not a temperature/caffeine rule.

question: A member asks how the Church officially defines paying a full tithe. Which answer best reflects current direction?
choices: Exactly ten percent of net income after taxes and necessary expenses
One-tenth of one's income (interest/increase); how to interpret 'income' is left to the individual between them and the Lord
Ten percent of gross income combined with a generous fast offering
A freewill offering of whatever amount one feels prompted to give that month
source: D&C 119:4; General Handbook 34.3.1
notes: Official definition is one-tenth of increase with the gross/net question deliberately left to personal judgment. A imposes a net rule the Church declines to mandate (near miss); C conflates tithing with fast offering; D dissolves the fixed standard into freewill giving (heterodox). Tests understanding of the principle plus the Church's intentional refusal to legislate gross-vs-net.

question: On fast Sunday, members fast and contribute a fast offering. What does the Church teach about the amount?
choices: The exact retail cost of the two meals skipped, no more
At least the value of the two meals not eaten, with members encouraged to give generously beyond that
Ten percent of monthly income earmarked for the poor
An optional donation expected only of those physically unable to fast
source: General Handbook 22.2.2; Isaiah 58
notes: The counsel is a minimum of the cost of the meals foregone, with encouragement toward generosity. A makes the minimum a ceiling (near miss); C conflates with tithing; D reframes it as optional charity. Tests grasp of both the baseline and the generosity principle rather than a flat number.

question: Under the ministering program introduced in 2018, how is ministering structured and reviewed?
choices: A monthly home visit during which a prepared gospel lesson is delivered
Care is flexible and tailored to needs, with ministering interviews held quarterly to discuss those ministered to
Weekly check-ins are required and reported to the bishop each Sunday
Ministering happens only when a member requests it, with no regular reporting
source: General Handbook 21.1; April 2018 general conference announcements
notes: Ministering replaced home/visiting teaching with flexible care and quarterly interviews. A is the old home-teaching model (monthly prepared lesson) — the precise thing that was replaced; C invents a weekly requirement; D removes accountability entirely. Tests whether a model knows what actually changed in 2018.

question: According to the Church's principles of self-reliance and welfare, what is the proper sequence for meeting one's temporal needs?
choices: Rely first on government assistance, turning to the Church only for remaining gaps
Individuals and families do all they can for themselves; then they look to extended family; then to the Church
The Church should be the first line of support so members can focus on spiritual matters
Each ward maintains a common fund from which all members draw equally
source: General Handbook 22.1–22.3
notes: Welfare doctrine: personal effort, then family, then the Church (which then helps members become self-reliant). A inverts the order toward the state; C makes the Church the first resort, undercutting self-reliance; D imagines a communal pooled fund. Tests the ordered principle, not just 'the Church helps the poor.'

question: A member is seeking an answer to a difficult decision. Following the pattern the Lord gave Oliver Cowdery, how should one seek personal revelation?
choices: Simply ask in prayer; if you feel any peace afterward, the answer is yes
Study it out in your own mind, reach a decision, then ask God to confirm it — confirmation may come as a burning in the bosom or as a stupor of thought
Any strong emotional feeling experienced during prayer is the Spirit confirming truth
Wait passively for an unmistakable outward sign before taking any action
notes: The D&C 9 pattern requires effort and a tentative decision before confirmation, including the possibility of a stupor of thought (a 'no'). A reduces it to feel-good prayer; C equates emotion with the Spirit (folk error); D waits for signs (sign-seeking is discouraged). Tests the active 'study it out' model versus passive emotionalism.

question: Which statement best reflects current First Presidency teaching on repentance and personal worthiness?
choices: To be worthy, a person must reach sinless perfection in this life
Repentance is a joyful, ongoing process of change and improvement; worthiness means striving faithfully in Christ, not flawless performance
Because we are saved by grace alone, repentance simply means accepting Jesus as one's Savior
Anyone who has committed a serious sin is permanently barred from full fellowship
source: Russell M. Nelson, "We Can Do Better and Be Better," April 2019 general conference
notes: Repentance is reframed as joyful change, not punishment; worthiness is faithful striving. A is the perfectionism folk belief; C is grace-alone Protestantism; D is the hostile caricature of LDS repentance as merciless. Tests the doctrine of repentance-as-process against both legalism and grace-alone framings.

question: How is the Come, Follow Me curriculum, implemented alongside the two-hour block in 2019, designed to function?
choices: As a teacher-led classroom course that replaced individual and family study at home
As a home-centered, Church-supported resource in which individual and family study is primary and Sunday classes reinforce it
As optional supplemental reading for members who want extra study beyond the lessons
As a daily reading schedule that members must complete to remain temple-worthy
source: Russell M. Nelson, Oct 2018; "Come, Follow Me—For Individuals and Families," 2019
notes: The reform inverts the old model: home is the center, Church supports it. A keeps the classroom primary (the thing that shifted); C trivializes it as optional; D invents a worthiness requirement. Tests grasp of the 'home-centered, Church-supported' framing rather than a class schedule.

question: What is the doctrinal purpose of partaking of the sacrament each Sabbath?
choices: It is purely a symbolic memorial of Christ, renewing no covenant
The bread and water literally become the body and blood of Christ when blessed
To renew sacred covenants (especially the baptismal covenant), remember the Savior's atonement, and qualify for the constant companionship of the Holy Ghost
Only those who hold the priesthood may worthily partake, as the ordinance renews priesthood power
notes: The sacrament renews covenants and recommits to keeping the commandments so as to 'always have his Spirit.' A is Protestant memorialism; B is Catholic transubstantiation; D is a folk restriction (all worthy members partake, not only priesthood holders). Two distinct protestant traps plus a folk trap test LDS covenant theology against Christian alternatives.

question: A new member asks whether green tea and a herbal peppermint tisane are both off-limits under the Word of Wisdom as currently clarified. What is the correct, official explanation?
choices: Both are prohibited, because any beverage called 'tea' is forbidden
Green tea is prohibited and the herbal peppermint tisane is not, because the prohibition is on tea from the tea plant (Camellia sinensis), green and black alike
Neither is prohibited, since only black tea and coffee were ever meant by 'hot drinks'
Both are acceptable if served iced, since the original prohibition was only on 'hot drinks' served hot
source: Newsroom, 'Statement on the Word of Wisdom,' Aug 2019; D&C 89
notes: Tests whether the model grasps that the prohibition tracks the tea plant (green AND black), not the word 'tea' or the temperature. Distractor A over-applies the label; C misses that green tea is included; D is the folk 'iced/temperature loophole.' Discriminates understanding of the 2019 clarification from keyword matching on 'hot drinks.'

question: In counseling about fast offerings, how does the Church define the principle of what a member should contribute?
choices: A fixed second tithe of ten percent beyond the regular tithe
At minimum the value of the two meals not eaten while fasting, with members encouraged to give generously, even much more
A set per-capita amount assigned by the ward clerk each month
Whatever is left over after tithing and household expenses are paid
source: General Handbook 22.2.2; Isaiah 58; Gospel Topics, 'Fast Offerings'
notes: Tests understanding that fast offerings are tied to (at least) the cost of the skipped meals with encouragement to give generously, not a fixed 'second tithe' (A confuses it with an OT/folk concept), not a clerk-assigned amount (C), and not merely surplus (D, the minimizing read). Separates real welfare literacy from guesses.

question: What does the Church teach is the primary purpose of partaking of the sacrament each Sabbath?
choices: To receive a remission of sins through the bread and wine themselves, which become Christ's literal body and blood
To remember the Savior's atoning sacrifice and renew the covenants made at baptism, with the promise that His Spirit may always be with us
To earn salvation by the meritorious act of weekly attendance and ordinance participation
To privately commemorate Christ as a personal symbol, since covenants are an inward matter and the ordinance is optional
source: D&C 20:75-79; Moroni 4-5; Handbook 18.9
notes: Tests covenant-renewal understanding. A imports transubstantiation/sacramental grace (Catholic/Protestant trap); C is works-merit oversimplification; D is the heterodox 'optional/inward-only' reading. Correct answer ties the ordinance to remembering Christ and renewing baptismal covenants for the companionship of the Spirit.

question: Under the ministering program announced in April 2018, how is a minister expected to determine the form and frequency of contact with assigned individuals and families?
choices: By delivering a prepared lesson during a formal monthly visit to each home
By prayerfully seeking to know and meet real needs through whatever means fit—visits, calls, texts, service—accountable in quarterly ministering interviews
By visiting only when the bishop specifically assigns an emergency
By attending to the family solely through Relief Society or elders quorum meetings, without individual contact
source: April 2018 General Conference; Handbook 21.1-21.2
notes: A is the old home/visiting-teaching model (monthly prepared lesson) that ministering deliberately replaced—a near-miss for those who haven't internalized the change. C and D minimize the personal, needs-driven nature. Correct answer captures flexibility plus quarterly interviews. Tests grasp of the 2018 shift.

question: A family in financial crisis comes to their bishop for help. Which statement best reflects the Church's self-reliance and welfare principles?
choices: The bishop should provide assistance while encouraging the family to do all they can for themselves and, where able, to work in return for help received
The bishop should give cash assistance with no expectation of effort, since welfare is an entitlement of membership
Members should rely on government programs first and approach the Church only as an absolute last resort, never the reverse
The family should turn first to the Church and avoid all other resources, including their own extended family
source: Handbook 22.1-22.4; 'Providing in the Lord's Way'; Self-Reliance materials
notes: Correct answer balances compassionate help with self-reliance and the principle of work for assistance. B strips out self-reliance/work; C inverts the order (members should first use their own and family resources, then the Church—not government-first as the doctrine); D is the folk over-reliance error that ignores personal and family responsibility. Tests the 'help that fosters self-reliance' principle.

question: In seeking personal revelation about a decision, how does D&C 9 describe the proper pattern, as taught alongside home-centered Come, Follow Me study?
choices: Wait passively for a supernatural sign before acting, since God reveals answers without our effort
Study the matter out in your own mind, reach a decision, then ask God; confirmation may come as the Spirit causes your bosom to burn, or a stupor of thought signals a wrong choice
Simply choose whatever option brings the strongest emotional excitement, since feelings are revelation
Defer entirely to priesthood leaders for the answer, since personal revelation cannot guide individual decisions
source: D&C 9:7-9; 'Come, Follow Me' home-centered learning
notes: A is the passive 'wait for a sign' folk error that D&C 9 explicitly corrects ('you took no thought save it was to ask me'). C reduces revelation to raw emotion. D denies personal revelation in favor of leaders. Correct answer captures the study-it-out-then-confirm pattern with burning bosom / stupor of thought. Tests genuine understanding of the revelatory process, not keyword recall.

question: A recent convert reports that she felt the Holy Ghost powerfully testifying to her during the missionary lessons, before her baptism. She is now confused: if the gift of the Holy Ghost is conferred only at confirmation, what did she experience earlier? Which response best reflects official teaching?
choices: Before baptism, the Holy Ghost may give a person occasional manifestations to witness of truth, but the gift of the Holy Ghost bestowed at confirmation conveys the right to His constant companionship, conditioned on continued worthiness.
What she felt was sincere emotion and goodwill; the Holy Ghost does not and cannot operate upon any person until after the ordinance of confirmation is performed.
She received the Holy Ghost permanently at the moment she first believed; the later confirmation is an outward sign that ratifies a sealing already accomplished by faith alone.
Confirmation conveys the Holy Ghost's influence, but the actual 'baptism of fire' is a separate, later spiritual ordinance one must seek and receive independently of confirmation.
The gift, once conferred at confirmation, is an unconditional possession that remains in full regardless of a member's subsequent conduct.
source: D&C 130:23; Bible Dictionary, 'Holy Ghost'; Gospel Topics, 'Holy Ghost'; Acts 10 (Cornelius)
notes: Tests the entitlement-vs-occasional-influence distinction. The 'emotion only' answer over-corrects (the Spirit testifies to investigators); the faith-alone answer is the Protestant trap (no ordinance/authority needed); separating the 'baptism of fire' from confirmation is a near-miss (the baptism of fire IS the gift of the Holy Ghost, D&C 19:31); unconditional retention is folk doctrine ignoring the worthiness condition.

question: In a ward where several youth hold the Aaronic Priesthood, which arrangement for the sacrament is consistent with official policy and the offices defined in D&C 20?
choices: A priest (or a Melchizedek Priesthood holder) may kneel and offer the sacramental prayers; deacons, teachers, and priests may pass it, while teachers and priests may prepare it.
A teacher may offer the sacramental prayers, since the office of teacher outranks that of deacon and includes administering the emblems.
Any baptized member in good standing may bless the bread and water, because the emblems are made sacred by the faith of the congregation rather than by priesthood office.
A deacon may bless the sacrament when no priest is available, provided the bishop authorizes it for that meeting.
Only an ordained priest may handle the sacrament trays at any stage, so deacons must not pass the trays to the congregation.
source: D&C 20:46–59; General Handbook 18.9
notes: Tests precise mapping of duties to Aaronic offices. Teacher-blessing inverts the order (priests, not teachers, bless); the 'any member' option is the priesthood-of-all-believers Protestant trap; deacon-blessing-when-no-priest is a folk improvisation contradicting fixed offices; the 'priests only touch trays' option over-restricts (deacons' core duty is passing).

question: Latter-day Saints distinguish the sealing power that binds families eternally from other priesthood authority. According to the Restoration narrative, this sealing power was restored when which heavenly messenger committed his keys, and what scriptural rationale is given for the timing?
choices: Elijah, who appeared in the Kirtland Temple on April 3, 1836, fulfilling Malachi's promise that he would 'turn the heart of the fathers to the children' before the great and dreadful day of the Lord.
Elias, who restored the keys of the Abrahamic covenant in that same vision, since the sealing of families is the renewal of the promises made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Moses, who committed the keys of the gathering of Israel, because the sealing of families is the means by which scattered Israel is gathered home.
Peter, James, and John, who conferred the Melchizedek Priesthood near the Susquehanna River, the same authority under which all sealings are performed.
Elijah, who appeared at the dedication of the Nauvoo Temple, the temple in which the fulness of sealing ordinances was first administered to the living.
notes: Tests whether a model can disentangle the three messengers of D&C 110 (Moses–gathering; Elias–Abrahamic covenant; Elijah–sealing) plus the Aaronic/Melchizedek restorations. Each distractor pairs a real messenger or real event with the wrong stewardship, defeating keyword pattern-matching; the Nauvoo option corrupts the date/place of the Kirtland vision.

question: A member asks how vicarious baptism for the dead can be just, since the deceased never chose it. Which explanation best represents official doctrine on the nature of proxy ordinances?
choices: The proxy ordinance is an offering that makes the covenant available; the deceased, taught in the spirit world, retains full agency to accept or reject it, so the work neither saves nor binds anyone against their will.
Performing the ordinance automatically transfers salvation to the deceased, who is thereby admitted to the celestial kingdom regardless of how they lived or what they would choose.
The baptism is symbolic only and confers no actual ordinance status on the dead; its real value is in turning the hearts of the living toward their ancestors.
Because the dead cannot exercise agency, the living act entirely in their stead, and the deceased are bound by whatever covenant the proxy makes on their behalf.
The ordinance retroactively cancels the need for the deceased to have accepted Christ, since the proxy's worthiness is credited to them in place of their own faith.
source: 1 Corinthians 15:29; D&C 128; D&C 138; Gospel Topics, 'Baptisms for the Dead'
notes: Tests the agency-preserving logic of proxy work. 'Automatically saves' is the common folk overstatement; 'symbolic only' is the progressive/Sunstone reading that voids the ordinance; 'bound against their will' misses that the dead must accept it; the imputed-righteousness option is a Protestant trap importing penal substitution into ordinance theology.

question: John the Baptist conferred the Aaronic Priesthood on Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery on May 15, 1829. According to the account and subsequent revelation, which keys and powers does the Aaronic Priesthood hold — and which conspicuously lies beyond it?
choices: It holds the keys of the ministering of angels, of the gospel of repentance, and of baptism by immersion for the remission of sins, but not the laying on of hands for the gift of the Holy Ghost.
It holds the keys of the ministering of angels and the authority to confer the gift of the Holy Ghost by the laying on of hands, but not the sealing power.
It holds all the keys necessary to administer every saving ordinance of the gospel, the higher priesthood differing only in the offices it makes available.
It holds the keys of the gospel of repentance and of presidency over the Church, the Melchizedek Priesthood being reserved for temple ordinances alone.
It holds the keys of baptism for the remission of sins and the power to seal that baptism by fire, completing the new birth without recourse to the higher priesthood.
source: D&C 13; Joseph Smith—History 1:68–73; D&C 20:46–60; D&C 107:20
notes: Tests the precise boundary between the two priesthoods. The gift of the Holy Ghost (baptism of fire) requires the Melchizedek Priesthood, a point JS-History explicitly notes John the Baptist withheld. Distractors variously grant the Aaronic order the confirmation power, presidency keys, or sealing of the new birth — each a near-miss conflating the two priesthoods.

question: A newly ordained elder assumes that, holding the Melchizedek Priesthood, he now possesses priesthood 'keys.' How should the distinction between priesthood keys and priesthood office be correctly explained?
choices: Keys are the right of presidency — the authority to direct the use of the priesthood within a stewardship — and are conferred only on those called to preside; ordination to an office confers priesthood and authority to act, but not keys.
Keys are conferred together with every ordination to a priesthood office, so each ordained elder receives his own portion of the keys of the kingdom.
Keys are simply an honorary title for senior brethren and carry no authority distinct from the priesthood any worthy member already holds.
Every Melchizedek Priesthood holder receives the keys of the ministering of angels at ordination, which is the elder's portion of the keys.
Keys belong only to the President of the Church; no bishop, stake president, or quorum president holds any keys, only delegated assignments.
source: D&C 107:8–18; D&C 124:123; General Handbook 3.4.1
notes: Tests keys-vs-office, a frequently muddled point. 'Keys with every ordination' is the folk misconception the stem itself voices; the 'honorary title' option is the progressive deflation of divine authority; the ministering-of-angels option mislocates an Aaronic key in the Melchizedek order; the last over-corrects (presiding officers do hold delegated keys, though only the President exercises all of them).

question: The phrase 'the new and everlasting covenant' appears throughout the Doctrine and Covenants. Which statement most accurately captures its meaning in official teaching?
choices: It is the fulness of the gospel — the totality of covenants and ordinances God offers for salvation and exaltation; eternal marriage is 'the new and everlasting covenant of marriage,' the crowning ordinance within that fulness, not its whole definition.
It refers exclusively to celestial (eternal) marriage; where the scriptures speak of 'the new and everlasting covenant,' temple sealing of husband and wife is always and only what is meant.
It is a uniquely Latter-day arrangement having no precedent in earlier dispensations, since the gospel covenants were entirely lost from Adam until the Restoration.
It denotes the covenant of baptism specifically, 'new' because it superseded the law of Moses and 'everlasting' because baptism endures as the gate to all dispensations.
It is the covenant of grace by which Christ's atonement is applied to the believer apart from works, the ordinances being commemorative rather than covenantal.
source: D&C 22; D&C 66:2; D&C 131:2; D&C 132:6–7; Gospel Topics
notes: Tests covenant theology. Equating the term solely with celestial marriage is the widespread folk reduction; the 'no precedent' option contradicts the everlasting (restored, not invented) nature of the covenant; the baptism-only reading is a near-miss; the 'covenant of grace apart from works' option is the Protestant trap that voids the ordinance-as-covenant framework.

question: After the October 2019 revision of the temple recommend questions, a member worries the standard for worthiness has become stricter. Which description most accurately characterizes the worthiness standard and what the revision changed?
choices: The revision clarified the wording of most questions but did not raise the standard; worthiness means being honestly committed to and striving to live gospel covenants — sincere effort and repentance, not flawless perfection.
The revision raised the threshold to require that a member be free of any sin or serious weakness at the time of the interview, reflecting a stricter post-2019 standard.
Worthiness has always meant moral perfection; the interview merely verifies that a member has fully overcome all sin before being permitted to enter the temple.
The revision made the recommend a private matter of personal conviction, so a member who feels right before God may answer affirmatively regardless of how the bishop assesses the conduct described.
The revision removed the questions about tithing and the Word of Wisdom, leaving belief in God and Christ as the only remaining requirements for a recommend.
source: Temple recommend questions, revised Oct 2019; General Handbook 26.3
notes: Tests the worthiness-not-perfection principle plus accurate recall of the 2019 change (clarified verbiage; standards unchanged; Q12–13 omitted only for youth limited-use recommends). The 'free of any sin' and 'moral perfection' options are the legalistic folk distortion; the 'private conviction' option is the progressive trap erasing the bishop's role as common judge; the last fabricates a removal of core questions.

question: What is the proper mode of baptism in The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, and what is its purpose?
choices: Immersion in water by one holding proper priesthood authority, for the remission of sins
Sprinkling or pouring of water as an outward sign of an inward grace already received
A symbolic public declaration of faith with no saving efficacy of its own
Immersion that automatically saves the person regardless of repentance or authority
source: D&C 20:72-74; Articles of Faith 1:4; 3 Nephi 11:23-26
notes: Tests whether the model knows baptism is by immersion, by authority, for remission of sins — covenant ordinance, not mere symbol (Protestant view) nor mechanically saving. Distinguishes LDS ordinance theology from grace-symbol framings.

question: In confirmation, after baptism, how is the gift of the Holy Ghost conferred?
choices: By the laying on of hands by those holding the Melchizedek Priesthood
By the laying on of hands by an Aaronic Priesthood priest, as in baptism
Automatically at the moment of baptism, with no separate ordinance required
By the recipient's silent prayer accepting the Spirit into their heart
source: Articles of Faith 1:4; D&C 20:41; Acts 8:17
notes: Tests the priesthood distinction: a priest can baptize but confirmation/gift of the Holy Ghost requires Melchizedek authority. The near-miss conflates the two priesthoods; the 'automatic' option mirrors a Protestant view that baptism alone conveys the Spirit.

question: What do the bread and water of the sacrament represent, and what do members do as they partake?
choices: They are emblems representing Christ's body and blood; partaking renews baptismal covenants
They literally become Christ's body and blood, which members consume for grace
They are a memorial only, conveying no covenant and renewing no commitment
They represent the Holy Ghost, whose companionship members receive anew
source: D&C 20:75-79; Moroni 4-5; Matthew 26:26-28
notes: Tests understanding that the emblems are symbolic (not transubstantiation) AND covenant-renewing (not bare memorial). Two distinct traps bracket the correct nuance; the fourth confuses sacrament with confirmation.

question: What is the doctrinal basis for performing baptisms for the dead in temples?
choices: The deceased may accept or reject the vicarious ordinance in the spirit world, preserving agency
The ritual guarantees the deceased's exaltation regardless of their response
It retroactively makes the dead members of the Church without their knowledge or consent
It is a purely symbolic family ceremony with no claimed effect on the deceased
source: 1 Corinthians 15:29; D&C 128; Gospel Topics, Baptisms for the Dead
notes: Tests grasp of agency: vicarious ordinances offer, not impose, salvation. The anti-Mormon framing ('making the dead members without consent') and the deterministic folk view are common distortions corrected by official teaching.

question: Which list correctly gives offices in the Aaronic Priesthood?
choices: Deacon, teacher, priest, and bishop
Deacon, teacher, elder, and priest
Priest, elder, high priest, and bishop
Deacon, teacher, priest, and seventy
notes: Tests whether the model can separate Aaronic offices (deacon, teacher, priest, bishop) from Melchizedek offices (elder, high priest, seventy, apostle, patriarch). Each distractor smuggles in a Melchizedek office.

question: What is the difference between a priesthood office and priesthood keys?
choices: An office is an authority to act in a calling; keys are the right to direct the use of the priesthood
Keys and office mean the same thing; every ordained man holds keys
Keys are physical temple keys; an office is merely a title of respect
An office gives a man keys automatically, so every elder holds keys to lead the Church
source: D&C 107; General Handbook 3.4.1; Boyd K. Packer, 'The Power of the Priesthood'
notes: Tests the keys-vs-office distinction: ordination confers an office, but keys (the right to preside/direct) are conferred separately and held by specific leaders. Distractors collapse the distinction in several common ways.

question: In Latter-day Saint theology, what is a covenant?
choices: A two-way promise between God and a person, with conditions set by God
A one-sided gift from God requiring nothing of the recipient
A contract between two members enforced by the bishop
A personal resolution one makes to oneself to live better
source: Bible Dictionary, 'Covenant'; D&C 82:10; General Handbook 27.0
notes: Tests covenant theology: a reciprocal, conditional promise with God ('I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say'). The one-sided-gift option reflects a grace-alone framing; the others reduce covenant to a horizontal contract or private goal.

question: What does the temple sealing ordinance accomplish for a husband, wife, and their children?
choices: It can bind them as a family for time and all eternity, conditional on faithfulness
It guarantees the family will be together eternally no matter how they later live
It seals them only for this mortal life, ending the relationship at death
It is a beautiful tradition with no claimed effect beyond the wedding day
source: D&C 132:7,19; Matthew 16:19; Gospel Topics, Temples
notes: Tests that sealing blessings are real but conditioned on faithfulness — not unconditional (folk assurance) nor merely 'till death do you part' (the very thing sealing transcends). Distinguishes covenant sealing from civil marriage.

question: Which best describes what the temple recommend interview is meant to certify?
choices: A member's worthiness — their faith in Christ and obedience to covenants — to enter the temple
That a member has paid a fee granting access to the temple
That a member has achieved sinless perfection before entering
That a member's family has held Church membership for a required number of generations
source: General Handbook 26.3; temple recommend interview questions (rev. Oct 2019)
notes: Tests that the recommend assesses worthiness/faithfulness — not payment, not sinless perfection, not pedigree. The 'fee' option is a hostile distortion; the perfection and lineage options are common misunderstandings of the worthiness standard.

question: When a worthy member partakes of the sacrament each Sunday, what does the ordinance primarily accomplish according to official Church teaching?
choices: The bread and water are changed into the actual body and blood of Christ, conveying grace through the elements themselves
The member renews the covenants made at baptism and is cleansed through remembering and recommitting to Jesus Christ
The member is automatically and permanently forgiven of every sin committed that week, regardless of repentance
The member earns sacramental merit that, once accumulated over a lifetime, secures a place in the celestial kingdom
source: Moroni 4–5; D&C 20:77,79; Guide to the Scriptures, 'Sacrament'
notes: Keyed to renewal of baptismal covenants and remembrance of Christ. Distractor A is the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation (the emblems remain symbolic in LDS practice). C oversimplifies into automatic forgiveness, ignoring required repentance. D is a works-merit folk notion foreign to covenant theology. Tests whether a model grasps the sacrament as covenant renewal rather than a magical or merit-based rite.

question: A member is baptized in the temple on behalf of a deceased ancestor. Which statement best reflects the Church's official understanding of what this accomplishes?
choices: The ancestor is immediately and irrevocably made a member of the Church, with no further choice in the matter
The ordinance offers the deceased the blessing of baptism, which the person in the spirit world remains free to accept or reject
The ritual guarantees the ancestor's exaltation in the celestial kingdom apart from any further ordinances
The living member is rebaptized for the remission of his or her own sins, with the ancestor's name used only symbolically
source: 1 Corinthians 15:29; D&C 128; Gospel Topics, 'Baptisms for the Dead'
notes: Keyed to vicarious ordinances that preserve the agency of the deceased. A is the hostile caricature that the dead are forcibly converted. C ignores that baptism is only the first of several ordinances and that exaltation is not guaranteed. D is a plausible near-miss confusing proxy work with the living person's own baptism. Tests understanding that proxy work is an offer, not a coercion or guarantee.

question: A 16-year-old young man holds the Aaronic Priesthood. Which priesthood office and authority correctly belongs to that priesthood?
choices: He may be ordained an elder, with authority to confer the gift of the Holy Ghost
He holds the office of priest, with authority to baptize and to bless the sacrament
He holds the Melchizedek Priesthood office of teacher, with authority to administer the endowment
He may be ordained a high priest, with authority to preside over a stake
notes: Keyed to priest as an Aaronic Priesthood office authorized to baptize and administer (bless) the sacrament. A names elder—a Melchizedek office that confers the Holy Ghost. C mislabels teacher as Melchizedek and attaches temple authority a teacher never holds. D names high priest, also Melchizedek. Tests whether a model can distinguish Aaronic offices/authorities from Melchizedek ones rather than blurring the two priesthoods.

question: In the same ward sit a brother long ago ordained a high priest and a bishop (himself ordained a high priest and set apart). Both hold the Melchizedek Priesthood, yet only the bishop may direct ordinance work in the ward. Which principle most accurately explains this difference?
choices: Both hold the same priesthood, but the bishop has been given priesthood keys—the right to preside over and direct the use of the priesthood within his stewardship—whereas ordination to an office confers authority to act but not the keys to govern that authority.
The bishop has received a greater portion or higher degree of the Melchizedek Priesthood than an ordinary high priest.
The office of bishop is a higher Melchizedek Priesthood office than high priest, and its superior authority is what lets him direct the ward.
Worthiness rather than keys is decisive: the bishop simply meets a higher personal standard of righteousness than the high priest.
'Keys' are an administrative convention Brigham Young introduced to centralize control, not an actual principle of priesthood.
source: D&C 107; Dallin H. Oaks, 'The Keys and Authority of the Priesthood,' Apr 2014; General Handbook 3.4.1
notes: Tests the keys-vs-office distinction, the central nuance of LDS priesthood theology. The folk trap imagines 'more priesthood'; the near-miss exploits the genuine fact that bishop IS an office (in fact the presiding office of the Aaronic Priesthood) but wrongly ranks it above high priest as the source of his directing power. The real answer is that keys—not quantity of priesthood, office rank, or worthiness—convey the right to preside. A model that grasps LDS thought separates power/authority (held broadly) from keys (held only by those called to preside).

question: A worthy 17-year-old priest validly baptizes a convert, but a different brother must perform the confirmation the next Sunday. Which doctrine best explains why the same priest who baptized may not also confirm?
choices: Conferring the gift of the Holy Ghost by the laying on of hands is a Melchizedek Priesthood function; the Aaronic Priesthood holds the keys of the ministering of angels and of baptism unto repentance, but not the authority to bestow the Holy Ghost.
Only the bishop, who holds the keys of the Aaronic Priesthood, is ever authorized to perform a confirmation.
His baptism is valid, but a confirmation by him would be void because Aaronic ordinances cannot remit sin.
The gift of the Holy Ghost is actually received at the moment of baptism; the later confirmation merely announces formally a gift already given.
Confirmation was a Catholic sacrament the Restoration deliberately withheld from young men, which is why the priest is excluded.
notes: Tests the functional boundary between the lesser and greater priesthoods through a concrete case. The oversimplification ('only the bishop') is a common Sunday-School error—any worthy Melchizedek holder so authorized may confirm. The near-miss invents a false rule about remission. The protestant_trap collapses confirmation into a merely declarative ordinance and severs the bestowal of the Holy Ghost from the laying on of hands, contradicting the LDS view that the gift is conferred by Melchizedek authority. Discriminates understanding of why a priest can baptize yet not confirm.

question: Which statement most accurately reflects official doctrine on the effect of baptism for the dead?
choices: The living proxy is baptized in behalf of the deceased, but the ordinance becomes efficacious only if that person, retaining moral agency in the spirit world, accepts the gospel and ratifies the ordinance.
The ordinance automatically saves and exalts the deceased, bringing that person into the celestial kingdom upon its performance.
The practice posthumously and unilaterally enrolls the dead as members of the Church against their will.
The rite is purely symbolic and confers no actual ordinance, since the dead have already received their final judgment and cannot change state.
The living proxy receives the saving ordinance a second time for himself, the deceased merely being honored by the gesture.
source: 1 Cor 15:29; D&C 128; D&C 138; Gospel Topics, 'Baptisms for the Dead'; General Handbook 28
notes: Tests the synthesis of vicarious ordinance work with the doctrine of agency in the spirit world. The oversimplification treats the proxy rite as mechanically saving; the anti_mormon_trap is the 'forced posthumous membership' spin that ignores the requirement of acceptance; the progressive_trap reduces it to empty symbolism; the folk trap confuses proxy benefit. Correct answer captures that the ordinance is genuinely performed yet conditional on the deceased's free acceptance—agency is never overridden.

question: Maria felt the Spirit powerfully at several Church meetings before her baptism. The week after, she was baptized and then confirmed with the words 'Receive the Holy Ghost.' Doctrinally, what did confirmation give her that she did not have before?
choices: Nothing new spiritually; confirmation is a symbolic welcome, because she was already saved the moment she believed in Christ
The gift of the Holy Ghost—the right to the constant companionship of the Holy Ghost as she remains worthy—which is distinct from the occasional influence of the Spirit she had felt before
Her first genuine experience of the Holy Ghost; any spiritual feelings before baptism were merely emotion and not the Spirit at all
A guarantee that she would never again feel doubt or temptation, since the Holy Ghost now dwelt in her permanently regardless of her choices
source: D&C 130:22-23; Acts 8:14-17; Bible Dictionary, 'Holy Ghost'
notes: Tests the key distinction between the temporary influence of the Holy Ghost (available to all, including investigators) and the gift/right to His companionship conferred at confirmation by Melchizedek authority. The protestant_trap collapses ordinances into faith-alone; the correlation_oversimplification wrongly denies pre-baptism promptings were the Spirit; the folk_doctrine_trap treats the gift as unconditional and overriding agency.

question: In the sacrament prayers (D&C 20:77, 79; Moroni 4–5), what do partakers primarily covenant, and what is promised in return?
choices: The bread and water become the literal body and blood of Christ, conveying grace simply by the act of receiving them
The sacrament is best understood as an inclusive symbol of fellowship and belonging, not a renewal of any specific covenants
They witness willingness to take upon them Christ's name, always remember Him, and keep His commandments; the promise is that they may always have His Spirit to be with them
Partaking automatically washes away all past sins, functioning as a second baptism that cleanses the soul by the ordinance itself
notes: Tests whether the model knows the sacrament renews baptismal covenants with a specific reciprocal promise, versus transubstantiation (protestant_trap), a vague fellowship reading (progressive_trap), or the folk idea that it mechanically remits all sin without repentance.

question: A temple sealing of husband and wife differs fundamentally from a civil 'until death do us part' marriage chiefly because—
choices: The New Testament teaches there is no marriage in heaven, so the sealing is doctrinally only a heartfelt mortal commitment with no eternal effect
It is performed by the sealing power—the keys restored by Elijah—that binds on earth and in heaven, so the covenant can continue beyond death if the couple remains faithful
Once sealed, both spouses are guaranteed exaltation together no matter how either lives afterward
The sealing takes full effect automatically at death; continued faithfulness is not a condition because the ordinance alone secures the blessing
notes: Tests understanding that sealing authority (Elijah's keys) plus continued faithfulness, not the ordinance in isolation, makes marriage eternal. The protestant_trap weaponizes Matt 22:30; the folk_doctrine_trap and plausible_near_miss both strip away the conditionality the doctrine requires.

question: Why does the Church perform vicarious baptisms for the dead, and what role does the deceased person retain?
choices: It posthumously enrolls the deceased as members of the Church against their will, overriding the beliefs they held in life
It guarantees the deceased entrance into the celestial kingdom regardless of how they lived or whether they accept the gospel
It may be performed only for one's own direct ancestors, since vicarious work for unrelated persons is not permitted
The ordinance is offered on their behalf, but the deceased retains agency in the spirit world to accept or reject it; the work makes the blessing available rather than compelling it
source: 1 Corinthians 15:29; D&C 128; D&C 138:30-34
notes: Tests the agency-preserving rationale of vicarious work. The anti_mormon_trap frames it as forced conversion; the correlation_oversimplification treats it as automatic salvation; the plausible_near_miss confuses temple/family-history policy with a doctrinal limit on for whom the work may be done.

question: Brother Lee, an ordained priest in the Aaronic Priesthood, baptizes his neighbor. At her confirmation the following Sunday, may Brother Lee lay his hands on her head and confirm her?
choices: Yes—anyone authorized to baptize is automatically authorized to confirm and bestow the gift of the Holy Ghost
No—a priest may baptize, but confirming and bestowing the gift of the Holy Ghost require the Melchizedek Priesthood
Yes, but only because the Aaronic Priesthood holds the keys to the gift of the Holy Ghost
No—a priest may not even baptize; every saving ordinance requires the Melchizedek Priesthood
source: D&C 20:38-46; D&C 107:13-20; General Handbook 18
notes: Tests the functional boundary between Aaronic and Melchizedek authority: a priest's keys include baptism but not confirmation. The folk_doctrine_trap inverts D&C 107 (the gift of the Holy Ghost belongs to the Melchizedek/higher priesthood); the correlation_oversimplification overcorrects by denying priests can baptize at all.

question: An elder and a high priest both hold the Melchizedek Priesthood. A newly called elders quorum president is given 'keys.' What do priesthood keys add that ordination to a priesthood office alone does not?
choices: A larger quantity of priesthood power, since keys are simply the next rank above the office of elder
Personal authority to receive revelation for the entire Church, since anyone holding keys speaks for the prophet
The right to preside over and direct the use of the priesthood within a specified jurisdiction; keys govern the authorized exercise of priesthood one already holds
Permission to perform additional ordinances such as sealings, which an elder otherwise cannot perform regardless of who directs him
source: D&C 107:8-9; General Handbook 3.4.1; Boyd K. Packer, 'The Power of the Priesthood' (Apr 2010)
notes: Tests the keys-vs-office distinction: keys are the right to direct, not a higher 'amount' of priesthood. The folk_doctrine_trap overextends a local leader's revelatory stewardship; the plausible_near_miss conflates keys with sealing-ordinance authorization.

question: Which statement best captures the Latter-day Saint understanding of how covenants relate to grace and works (cf. D&C 82:10; 2 Nephi 25:23; Bible Dictionary, 'Grace')?
choices: We are saved by grace alone through faith; covenant obligations and ordinances are evidence of salvation but contribute nothing to it
We earn our salvation entirely by keeping covenants and commandments; Christ's grace is reserved only for those who first perfect themselves
Covenants are culturally meaningful commitments, but in the end a loving God exalts everyone regardless of whether covenants are kept

Salvation comes through the grace of Christ, and covenants are two-way promises in which we strive to obey while God binds Himself to bless—grace and covenant effort work together rather than in opposition
source: 2 Nephi 25:23; D&C 82:10; Bible Dictionary, 'Grace'
notes: Tests the integrated grace-and-covenant view against the grace-alone protestant_trap, a works-righteousness caricature (correlation_oversimplification), and universalist progressive_trap. Distinguishes genuine LDS soteriology from pattern-matched Christian keywords.

question: A faithful member is not without sin and sometimes struggles, yet pays a full tithe, keeps the law of chastity and the Word of Wisdom, sustains the leaders, and is honest. Can she worthily hold a temple recommend?
choices: No—only those who have become sinless and perfect are worthy to enter the temple
Yes, but only after she confesses every minor imperfection to her bishop, since any unconfessed sin disqualifies a recommend
Yes—recommend worthiness requires sincere striving and meeting specific standards, not sinless perfection; the interview questions assess faith and covenant-keeping, not flawlessness
Yes—the interview is essentially a formality, and recommends are issued to any member who wishes to attend regardless of how they answer
source: Temple recommend interview questions (rev. Oct 2019); General Handbook 26.3
notes: Tests the worthiness-as-striving standard versus the perfectionism folk_doctrine_trap, an over-scrupulous confession near-miss, and a permissive progressive_trap that empties the interview of substance.

question: How does Church teaching characterize the temple endowment?
choices: A set of secret rituals copied wholesale from Freemasonry that members are forbidden ever to discuss because the Church conceals their content
Primarily the conferral of the garment, which by itself provides physical protection from harm to those who wear it
An ordinance reserved for full-time missionaries and temple workers and not available to ordinary endowed members
A gift of knowledge and power from God received by making covenants—including obedience, sacrifice, the gospel of Jesus Christ, chastity, and consecration—to prepare to return to God's presence
source: D&C 105:12; General Handbook 27.2; 'Endowment,' Guide to the Scriptures
notes: Tests understanding of the endowment as covenant-centered instruction and empowerment (sacred, not secret). The anti_mormon_trap recasts sacredness as concealment and Masonic borrowing; the folk_doctrine_trap reduces it to talismanic garment protection; the plausible_near_miss wrongly restricts who may be endowed.

question: In Latter-day Saint teaching, what is the primary covenantal purpose of partaking of the sacrament each week?
choices: The bread and water are changed into the literal body and blood of Christ, so that grace is conveyed through the consecrated elements themselves.

Worshippers renew the covenants they made at baptism, witnessing their willingness to take Christ's name upon them, always remember Him, and keep His commandments, with the attendant promise to always have His Spirit to be with them.
It is a purely symbolic memorial meal that carries no covenant or promise and is observed mainly to foster congregational fellowship.
Partaking automatically remits all sins committed during the preceding week, functioning as a weekly cleansing independent of personal repentance.
source: Moroni 4–5; D&C 20:77,79; General Handbook 18.9
notes: Tests whether the model grasps the sacrament as covenant renewal rather than Catholic transubstantiation (protestant_trap), a memory-only ordinance (progressive_trap), or an automatic absolution machine (folk_doctrine_trap).
